334Chapter 10: Mopoly
Start Up: Surrounded by Mopolies
If your college or university is like most, you spend a lot of time, and money, dealing with firms that face little competi. Your campus bookstore is likely to be the only local firm selling the texts that professors require you to read. Your school may have granted an exclusive franchise to a single firm for food service and to ather firm for vending machines. A single firm may provide your utilities—electricity, natural gas, and water.
Unlike the individual firms we have previously studied that operate in a competitive market, taking the price, which is determined by demand and supply, as given, in this chapter we investigate the behavior of firms that have their markets all to themselves. As the only suppliers of particular goods or services, they face the downward-sloping market demand curve alone.
We will find that firms that have their markets all to themselves behave in a manner that is in many respects different from the behavior of firms in perfect competi. Such firms continue to use the marginal decision rule in maximizing profits, but their freedom to select from the price and quantity combinas given by the market demand curve affects the way in which they apply this rule.
We will show that a mopoly firm is likely to produce less and charge more for what it produces than firms in a competitive industry. As a result, a mopoly solu is likely to be inefficient from society’s perspective. We will explore the policy alternatives available to government agencies in dealing with mopoly firms. First, though, we will look at characteristics of mopoly and at condis that give rise to mopolies in the first place.
335 10.2 The Mopoly Model
Learning Objectives
Explain the relaship between price and marginal revenue when a firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
Explain the relaship between marginal revenue and elasticity along a linear demand curve.
Apply the marginal decision rule to explain how a mopoly maximizes profit.
Analyzing choices is a more complex challenge for a mopoly firm than for a perfectly competitive firm. After all, a competitive firm takes the market price as given and determines its profit-maximizing output. Because a mopoly has its market all to itself, it can determine t only its output but its price as well. What kinds of price and output choices will such a firm make?
We will answer that ques in the context of the marginal decision rule: a firm will produce addial units of a good until marginal revenue equals marginal cost. To apply that rule to a mopoly firm, we must first investigate the special relaship between demand and marginal revenue for a mopoly.
Mopoly and Market Demand
Because a mopoly firm has its market all to itself, it faces the market demand curve. figureure 10.3 “Perfect Competi Versus Mopoly” compares the demand situas faced by a mopoly and a perfectly competitive firm. In Panel (a), the equilibrium price for a perfectly competitive firm is determined by the intersec of the demand and supply curves. The market supply curve is found simply by summing the supply curves of individual firms. Those, in turn, consist of the pors of marginal cost curves that lie above the average variable cost curve. The marginal cost curve, MC, for a single firm is illustrated. tice the break in the horizontal axis indicating that the quantity produced by a single firm is a trivially small frac of the whole. In the perfectly competitive model, one firm has thing to do with the determina of the market price. Each firm in a perfectly competitive industry faces a horizontal demand curve defined by the market price.
figureure 10.3 Perfect Competi Versus Mopoly Panel (a) shows the determina of equilibrium price and output in a perfectly competitive market. A typical firm with marginal cost curve MC is a price taker, choosing to produce quantity q at the equilibrium price P. In Panel (b) a mopoly faces a downward-sloping market demand curve. As a profit maximizer, it determines its profit-maximizing output. Once it determines that quantity, however, the price at which it can sell that output is found from the demand curve. The mopoly firm can sell addial units only by lowering price. The perfectly competitive firm, by contrast, can sell any quantity it wants at the market price.
336
Contrast the situa shown in Panel (a) with the one faced by the mopoly firm in Panel (b). Because it is the only supplier in the industry, the mopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand curve alone. It may choose to produce any quantity. But, unlike the perfectly competitive firm, which can sell all it wants at the going market price, a mopolist can sell a greater quantity only by cutting its price.
Suppose, for example, that a mopoly firm can sell quantity Q1 units at a price P1 in Panel (b). If it wants to increase its output to Q2 units—and sell that quantity—it must reduce its price to P2. To sell quantity Q3 it would have to reduce the price to P3. The mopoly firm may choose its price and output, but it is restricted to a combina of price and output that lies on the demand curve. It could t, for example, charge price P1 and sell quantity Q3. To be a price setter, a firm must face a downward-sloping demand curve.
Total Revenue and Price Elasticity
A firm’s elasticity of demand with respect to price has important implicas for assessing the impact of a price change on total revenue. Also, the price elasticity of demand can be different at different points on a firm’s demand curve. In this sec, we shall see why a mopoly firm will always select a price in the elastic region of its demand curve.
Suppose the demand curve facing a mopoly firm is given by Equa 10.1, where Q is the quantity demanded per unit of time and P is the price per unit:
Equa 10.1
Q=10−P 337
This demand equa implies the demand schedule shown in figureure 10.4 “Demand, Elasticity, and Total Revenue”. Total revenue for each quantity equals the quantity times the price at which that quantity is demanded. The mopoly firm’s total revenue curve is given in Panel (b). Because a mopolist must cut the price of every unit in order to increase sales, total revenue does t always increase as output rises. In this case, total revenue reaches a maximum of $25 when 5 units are sold. Beyond 5 units, total revenue begins to decline.
figureure 10.4 Demand& Elasticity& and Total Revenue Suppose a mopolist faces the downward-sloping demand curve shown in Panel (a). In order to increase the quantity sold& it must cut the price. Total revenue is found by multiplying the price and quantity sold at each price. Total revenue& plotted in Panel (b)& is maximized at $25& when the quantity sold is 5 units and the price is $5. At that point on the demand curve& the price elasticity of demand equals −1.
The demand curve in Panel (a) of figureure 10.4 “Demand& Elasticity& and Total Revenue” shows ranges of values of the price elasticity of demand. We have learned that price elasticity varies along a linear demand curve in a special way: Demand is price elastic at points in the upper half of the demand curve and price inelastic in the lower half of the demand curve. If demand is price elastic& a price reduc increases total revenue. To sell an addial unit& a mopoly firm must lower its price. The sale of one more unit will increase revenue because the percentage increase in the quantity demanded exceeds the percentage decrease in the price. The elastic range of the demand curve corresponds to the range over which the total revenue curve is rising in Panel (b) of figureure 10.4 “Demand& Elasticity& and Total Revenue”.
If demand is price inelastic& a price reduc reduces total revenue because the percentage increase in the quantity demanded is less than the percentage decrease in the price. Total revenue falls as the firm sells addial units over the inelastic range of the demand curve. The downward-sloping por of the total revenue curve in Panel (b) corresponds to the inelastic range of the demand curve.338
That point on the total revenue curve in Panel (b) corresponds to the point at which total revenue reaches its maximum.
The relaship among price elasticity& demand& and total revenue has an important implica for the selec of the profit-maximizing price and output: A mopoly firm will never choose a price and output in the inelastic range of the demand curve. Suppose& for example& that the mopoly firm represented in figureure 10.4 “Demand& Elasticity& and Total Revenue” is charging $3 and selling 7 units. Its total revenue is thus $21. Because this combina is in the inelastic por of the demand curve& the firm could increase its total revenue by raising its price. It could& at the same time& reduce its total cost. Raising price means reducing output; a reduc in output would reduce total cost. If the firm is operating in the inelastic range of its demand curve& then it is t maximizing profits. The firm could earn a higher profit by raising price and reducing output. It will continue to raise its price until it is in the elastic por of its demand curve. A profit-maximizing mopoly firm will therefore always operate at a price and output combina in the elastic range of its demand curve.
Of course& the firm could choose a point at which demand is unit price elastic. At that point& total revenue is maximized. But the firm seeks to maximize profit& t total revenue. A solu that maximizes total revenue will t maximize profit unless marginal cost is zero.
Demand and Marginal Revenue
In the perfectly competitive case& the addial revenue a firm gains from selling an addial unit—its marginal revenue—is equal to the market price. The firm’s demand curve& which is a horizontal line at the market price& is also its marginal revenue curve. But a mopoly firm can sell an addial unit only by lowering the price. That fact complicates the relaship between the mopoly’s demand curve and its marginal revenue.
Suppose the firm in figureure 10.4 “Demand& Elasticity& and Total Revenue” sells 2 units at a price of $8 per unit. Its total revenue is $16. w it wants to sell a third unit and wants to kw the marginal revenue of that unit. To sell 3 units rather than 2& the firm must lower its price to $7 per unit. Total revenue rises to $21. The marginal revenue of the third unit is thus $5. But the price at which the firm sells 3 units is $7. Marginal revenue is less than price.
To see why the marginal revenue of the third unit is less than its price& we need to examine more carefully how the sale of that unit affects the firm’s revenues. The firm brings in $7 from the sale of the third unit. But selling the third unit required the firm to charge a price of $7 instead of the $8 the firm was charging for 2 units. The firm receives less for the first 2 units. The marginal revenue of the third unit is the $7 the firm receives for that unit minus the $1 reduc in revenue for each of the first two units. The marginal revenue of the third unit is thus $5. (In this chapter we assume that the mopoly firm sells all units of output at the same price. In the next chapter& we will look at cases in which firms charge different prices to different customers.)
Marginal revenue is less than price for the mopoly firm. figureure 10.5 “Demand and Marginal Revenue” shows the relaship between demand and marginal revenue& based on the demand curve introduced in figureure 10.4 “Demand& Elasticity& and Total Revenue”. As always& we follow the conven of plotting marginal values at the midpoints of the intervals.339
figureure 10.5 Demand and Marginal Revenue The marginal revenue curve for the mopoly firm lies below its demand curve. It shows the addial revenue gained from selling an addial unit. tice that& as always& marginal values are plotted at the midpoints of the respective intervals.
When the demand curve is linear& as in figureure 10.5 “Demand and Marginal Revenue”& the marginal revenue curve 340can be placed according to the following rules: the marginal revenue curve is always below the demand curve and will bisect any horizontal line drawn between the vertical axis and the demand curve. To put it ather way& the marginal revenue curve will be twice as steep as the demand curve. The demand curve in figureure 10.5 “Demand and Marginal Revenue” is given by the equa Q=10−P& which can be written P=10−Q. The marginal revenue curve is given by P=10−2Q& which is twice as steep as the demand curve.
The marginal revenue and demand curves in figureure 10.5 “Demand and Marginal Revenue” follow these rules. The marginal revenue curve lies below the demand curve& and it bisects any horizontal line drawn from the vertical axis to the demand curve. At a price of $6& for example& the quantity demanded is 4. The marginal revenue curve passes through 2 units at this price. At a price of 0& the quantity demanded is 10; the marginal revenue curve passes through 5 units at this point.
Just as there is a relaship between the firm’s demand curve and the price elasticity of demand& there is a relaship between its marginal revenue curve and elasticity. Where marginal revenue is positive& demand is price elastic. Where marginal revenue is negative& demand is price inelastic. Where marginal revenue is zero& demand is unit price elastic.
When marginal revenue is … then demand is …
positive& price elastic.
negative& price inelastic.
zero& unit price elastic.
A firm would t produce an addial unit of output with negative marginal revenue. And& assuming that the produc of an addial unit has some cost& a firm would t produce the extra unit if it has zero marginal revenue. Because a mopoly firm will generally operate where marginal revenue is positive& we see once again that it will operate in the elastic range of its demand curve.
Mopoly Equilibrium: Applying the Marginal Decision Rule
Profit-maximizing behavior is always based on the marginal decision rule: Addial units of a good should be produced as long as the marginal revenue of an addial unit exceeds the marginal cost. The maximizing solu occurs where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. As always& firms seek to maximize ecomic profit& and costs are measured in the ecomic sense of opportunity cost.
figureure 10.6 “The Mopoly Solu” shows a demand curve and an associated marginal revenue curve for a mopoly firm. The marginal cost curve is like those we derived earlier; it falls over the range of output in which the firm experiences increasing marginal returns& then rises as the firm experiences diminishing marginal returns.
figureure 10.6 The Mopoly Solu The mopoly firm maximizes profit by producing an output Qm at point G& where the marginal revenue and marginal cost curves intersect. It sells this output at price Pm.
341
To determine the profit-maximizing output& we te the quantity at which the firm’s marginal revenue and marginal cost curves intersect (Qm in figureure 10.6 “The Mopoly Solu”). We read up from Qm to the demand curve to find the price Pm at which the firm can sell Qm units per period. The profit-maximizing price and output are given by point E on the demand curve.
Thus we can determine a mopoly firm’s profit-maximizing price and output by following three steps:
Determine the demand& marginal revenue& and marginal cost curves.
Select the output level at which the marginal revenue and marginal cost curves intersect.
Determine from the demand curve the price at which that output can be sold.
figureure 10.7 Computing Mopoly Profit A mopoly firm’s profit per unit is the difference between price and average total cost. Total profit equals profit per unit times the quantity produced. Total profit is given by the area of the shaded rectangle ATCmPmEF.
342
Once we have determined the mopoly firm’s price and output& we can determine its ecomic profit by adding the firm’s average total cost curve to the graph showing demand& marginal revenue& and marginal cost& as shown in figureure 10.7 “Computing Mopoly Profit”. The average total cost (ATC) at an output of Qm units is ATCm. The firm’s profit per unit is thus Pm – ATCm. Total profit is found by multiplying the firm’s output& Qm& by profit per unit& so total profit equals Qm(Pm – ATCm)—the area of the shaded rectangle in figureure 10.7 “Computing Mopoly Profit”.
Heads Up!
Dispelling Myths About Mopoly
Three common misconceps about mopoly are:
Because there are rivals selling the products of mopoly firms& they can charge whatever they want.
Mopolists will charge whatever the market will bear.
Because mopoly firms have the market to themselves& they are guaranteed huge profits.
As figureure 10.6 “The Mopoly Solu” shows& once the mopoly firm decides on the number of units of output that will maximize profit& the price at which it can sell that many units is found by “reading off” the demand curve the price associated with that many units. If it tries to sell Qm units of output for more than Pm& some of its output will go unsold. The mopoly firm can set its price& but is restricted to price and output combinas that lie on its demand curve. It cant just “charge whatever it wants.” And if it charges “all the market will bear&” it will sell either 0 or& at most& 1 unit of output. 343
Neither is the mopoly firm guaranteed a profit. Consider figureure 10.7 “Computing Mopoly Profit”. Suppose the average total cost curve& instead of lying below the demand curve for some output levels as shown& were instead everywhere above the demand curve. In that case& the mopoly will incur losses matter what price it chooses& because average total cost will always be greater than any price it might charge. As is the case for perfect competi& a mopoly firm can keep producing in the short run so long as price exceeds average variable cost. In the long run& it can stay in business only if it can cover all of its costs.
Key Takeaways
If a firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve& marginal revenue is less than price.
Marginal revenue is positive in the elastic range of a demand curve& negative in the inelastic range& and zero where demand is unit price elastic.
If a mopoly firm faces a linear demand curve& its marginal revenue curve is also linear& lies below the demand curve& and bisects any horizontal line drawn from the vertical axis to the demand curve.
To maximize profit or minimize losses& a mopoly firm produces the quantity at which marginal cost equals marginal revenue. Its price is given by the point on the demand curve that corresponds to this quantity.

Case in Point: Profit-Maximizing Hockey Teams
figureure 10.8 Duluoz cats – face off – CC BY-NC-ND 2.0.

Love of the game? Love of the city? Are those the factors that influence owners of professional sports teams in setting admissions prices? Four ecomists at the University of Vancouver have what they think is the answer for one group of teams: professional hockey teams set admission prices at levels that maximize their profits. They regard hockey teams as mopoly firms and use the mopoly model to examine the team’s behavior.
The ecomists& Donald G. Ferguson& Kenneth G. Stewart& John Colin H. Jones& and Andre Le Dressay& used data from three seasons to estimate demand and marginal revenue curves facing each team in the Naal Hockey League. They found that demand for a team’s tickets is affected by popula and income in the team’s home city& the team’s standing in the Naal Hockey League& and the number of superstars on the team.
Because a sports team’s costs do t vary significantly with the number of fans who attend a given game& the ecomists assumed that marginal cost is zero. The profit-maximizing number of seats sold per game is thus the quantity at which marginal revenue is zero& provided a team’s stadium is large eugh to hold that quantity of fans. This unconstrained quantity is labeled Qu& with a corresponding price Pu in the graph.
Stadium size and the demand curve facing a team might prevent the team from selling the profit-maximizing quantity of tickets. If its stadium holds only Qc fans& for example& the team will sell that many tickets at price Pc; its marginal revenue is positive at that quantity. Ecomic theory thus predicts that the marginal revenue for teams that consistently sell out their games will be positive& and the marginal revenue for other teams will be zero.
The ecomists’ statistical results were consistent with the theory. They found that teams that don’t typically sell out their games operate at a quantity at which marginal revenue is about zero& and that teams with sellouts have positive marginal revenue. “It’s clear that these teams are very sophisticated in their use of pricing to maximize profits&” Mr. Ferguson said.

Learning Objectives

We have seen that for mopolies pursuing profit maximiza& the outcome differs from the case of perfect competi. Does this matter to society? In this sec& we will focus on the differences that stem from market structure and assess their implicas.
Efficiency& Equity& and Concentra of Power
A mopoly firm determines its output by setting marginal cost equal to marginal revenue. It then charges the price at which it can sell that output& a price determined by the demand curve. That price exceeds marginal revenue; it therefore exceeds marginal cost as well. That contrasts with the case in perfect competi& in which price and marginal cost are equal. The higher price charged by a mopoly firm may allow it a profit—in part at the expense of consumers& whose reduced ops may give them little say in the matter. The mopoly solu thus raises problems of efficiency& equity& and the concentra of power.
Mopoly and Efficiency
The fact that price in mopoly exceeds marginal cost suggests that the mopoly solu violates the basic condi for ecomic efficiency& that the price system must confront decision makers with all of the costs and all of the benefits of their choices. Efficiency requires that consumers confront prices that equal marginal costs. Because a mopoly firm charges a price greater than marginal cost& consumers will consume less of the mopoly’s good or service than is ecomically efficient.
To contrast the efficiency of the perfectly competitive outcome with the inefficiency of the mopoly outcome& imagine a perfectly competitive industry whose solu is depicted in figureure 10.11 “Perfect Competi& Mopoly& and Efficiency”. The short-run industry supply curve is the summa of individual marginal cost curves; it may be regarded as the marginal cost curve for the industry. A perfectly competitive industry achieves equilibrium at point C& at price Pc and quantity Qc.348
figureure 10.11 Perfect Competi& Mopoly& and Efficiency Given market demand and marginal revenue& we can compare the behavior of a mopoly to that of a perfectly competitive industry. The marginal cost curve may be thought of as the supply curve of a perfectly competitive industry. The perfectly competitive industry produces quantity Qc and sells the output at price Pc. The mopolist restricts output to Qm and raises the price to Pm. Reorganizing a perfectly competitive industry as a mopoly results in a deadweight loss to society given by the shaded area GRC. It also transfers a por of the consumer surplus earned in the competitive case to the mopoly firm.
w& suppose that all the firms in the industry merge and a government restric prohibits entry by any new firms. Our perfectly competitive industry is w a mopoly. Assume the mopoly continues to have the same marginal cost and demand curves that the competitive industry did. The mopoly firm faces the same market demand curve& from which it derives its marginal revenue curve. It maximizes profit at output Qm and charges price Pm. Output is lower and price higher than in the competitive solu.
Society would gain by moving from the mopoly solu at Qm to the competitive solu at Qc. The benefit to consumers would be given by the area under the demand curve between Qm and Qc; it is the area QmRCQc. An increase in output& of course& has a cost. Because the marginal cost curve measures the cost of each addial unit& we can think of the area under the marginal cost curve over some range of output as measuring the total cost of that output. Thus& the total cost of increasing output from Qm to Qc is the area under the marginal cost curve over that range—the area QmGCQc. Subtracting this cost from the benefit gives us the net gain of moving from 349the mopoly to the competitive solu; it is the shaded area GRC. That is the potential gain from moving to the efficient solu. The area GRC is a deadweight loss.
Mopoly and Equity
The mopoly solu raises issues t just of efficiency but also of equity. figureure 10.11 “Perfect Competi& Mopoly& and Efficiency” shows that the mopolist charges price Pm rather than the competitive price Pc. The higher price charged by the mopoly firm reduces consumer surplus. Consumer surplus is the difference between what consumers are willing to pay for a good and what they actually pay. It is measured by the area under the demand curve and above the price of the good over the range of output produced.
If the industry were competitive& consumer surplus would be the area below the demand curve and above Pc. With mopoly& consumer surplus would be the area below the demand curve and above PmR. Part of the reduc in consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve between Qc and Qm; it is contained in the deadweight loss area GRC. But consumers also lose the area of the rectangle bounded by the competitive and mopoly prices and by the mopoly output; this lost consumer surplus is transferred to the mopolist.
The fact that society suffers a deadweight loss due to mopoly is an efficiency problem. But the transfer of a por of consumer surplus to the mopolist is an equity issue. Is such a transfer legitimate? After all& a mopoly firm enjoys a privileged posi& protected by barriers to entry from competi. Should it be allowed to extract these gains from consumers? We will see that public policy suggests that the answer is . Regulatory efforts imposed in mopoly cases often seek to reduce the degree to which mopoly firms extract consumer surplus from consumers by reducing the prices these firms charge.
Mopoly and the Concentra of Power
The objecs to mopoly run much deeper than worries over ecomic efficiency and high prices. Because a mopoly enjoys barriers that block potential rivals& a mopoly firm wields considerable market power. For many people& that concentra of power is objecable. A decentralized& competitive market constantly tests the ability of firms to satisfy consumers& pushes them to find new products and new and better produc methods& and wipes away ecomic profits. Firms that operate in the shelter of mopoly may be largely immune to such pressures. Consumers are likely to be left with fewer choices& higher costs& and lower quality.
Perhaps more important in the view of many ecomists is the fact that the existence of ecomic profits provides both an incentive and the means for mopolists to aggressively protect their posi and extend it if possible. These ecomists point out that mopolists may be willing to spend their ecomic profits in attempts to influence political leaders and public authorities (including regulatory authorities) who can help them maintain and enhance their mopoly posi. Graft and corrup may be the result& claim these critics. Indeed& Microsoft has been accused by its rivals of bullying computer manufacturers into installing its web browser& Internet Explorer& exclusively on their computers.
Attitudes about Microsoft reflect these concerns. Even among people who feel that its products are good and350 will it charge more for its products? Will it continue to invate?
Public Policy Toward Mopoly
Pulling together what we have learned in this chapter on mopoly and previously on perfect competi& Table 10.1 “Characteristics of Perfect Competi and Mopoly” summarizes the differences between the models of perfect competi and mopoly. Most importantly we te that whereas the perfectly competitive firm is a price taker& the mopoly firm is a price setter. Because of this difference& we can object to mopoly on grounds of ecomic efficiency; mopolies produce too little and charge too much. Also& the high price and persistent profits strike many as inequitable. Others may simply see mopoly as an unacceptable concentra of power.

Characteristic or Event Perfect Competi Mopoly

Public policy toward mopoly generally recognizes two important dimensions of the mopoly problem. On the one hand& the combining of competing firms into a mopoly creates an inefficient and& to many& inequitable solu. On the other hand& some industries are characterized as natural mopolies; produc by a single firm allows ecomies of scale that result in lower costs.
The combining of competing firms into a mopoly firm or unfairly driving competitors out of business is generally forbidden in the United States. Regulatory efforts to prevent mopoly fall under the purview of the na’s antitrust laws& discussed in more detail in a later chapter.
At the same time& we must be careful to avoid the mistake of simply assuming that competi is the alternative to mopoly& that every mopoly can and should be replaced by a competitive market. One key source of mopoly351 power& after all& is ecomies of scale. In the case of natural mopoly& the alternative to a single firm is many small& high-cost producers. We may t like having only one local provider of water& but we might like even less having dozens of providers whose costs—and prices—are higher. Where mopolies exist because ecomies of scale prevail over the entire range of market demand& they may serve a useful ecomic role. We might want to regulate their produc and pricing choices& but we may t want to give up their cost advantages.
Where a natural mopoly exists& the price charged by the firm and other aspects of its behavior may be subject to regula. Water or natural gas& for example& are often distributed by a public utility—a mopoly firm whose prices are regulated by a state or local government agency. Typically& such agencies seek to force the firm to charge lower prices& and to make less profit& than it would otherwise seek.
Although ecomists are hesitant to levy blanket condemnas of mopoly& they are generally sharply critical of mopoly power where raale for it exists. When firms have substantial mopoly power only as a result of government policies that block entry& there may be little defense for their mopoly posis.
Public policy toward mopoly aims generally to strike the balance implied by ecomic analysis. Where raales exist& as in the case of natural mopoly& mopolies are permitted—and their prices are regulated. In other cases& mopoly is prohibited outright. Societies are likely to at least consider taking ac of some kind against mopolies unless they appear to offer cost or other techlogical advantages.
The Fragility of Mopoly Power
An important factor in thinking about public policy toward mopoly is to recognize that mopoly power can be a fleeting thing. Firms constantly seek out the market power that mopoly offers. When condis allow to achieve this power& firms that succeed in carving out mopoly posis enjoy substantial profits. The potential for high profits invites continuing attempts to break down the barriers to entry that insulate mopolies from competi.
Techlogical change and the pursuit of profits chip away constantly at the entrenched power of mopolies. Breathtaking techlogical change has occurred in the telecommunicas industry. Catalog companies are challenging the mopoly posis of some retailers; internet booksellers and online textbook companies like gone.2012books.lardbucket.org are challenging the mopoly power of your university’s bookstore; and Federal Express& UPS& and other companies are taking on the U.S. Postal Service. The assaults on mopoly power are continuous. Thus& even the mopoly firm must be on the lookout for potential competitors.
Potential rivals are always beating at the door and thereby making the mopoly’s fragile posi contestable—that is& open to entry& at least in the sense of rival firms producing “close eugh&” if t identical& substitutes—close eugh that they might eliminate the firm’s mopoly power.
Key Takeaways
A mopoly firm produces an output that is less than the efficient level. The result is a deadweight loss to352 society& given by the area between the demand and marginal cost curves over the range of output between the output chosen by the mopoly firm and the efficient output.
The higher price charged by the mopoly firm compared to the perfectly competitive firm reduces consumer surplus& part of which is transferred to the mopolist. This transfer generates an equity issue.
The mopoly firm’s market power reduces consumers’ choices and may result in higher prices& but there may be advantages to mopoly as well& such as ecomies of scale and techlogical invas encouraged by the patent system.
Public policy toward mopoly consists of antitrust laws and regula of natural mopolies.
Forces that limit the power of mopoly firms are the constant effort by other firms to capture some of the mopoly firm’s profits and techlogical change that erodes mopoly power.

Summary
This chapter has examined the profit-maximizing behavior of mopoly firms. Mopoly occurs if an industry consists of a single firm and entry into that industry is blocked.
Potential sources of mopoly power include the existence of ecomies of scale over the range of market demand& locaal advantages& high sunk costs associated with entry& restricted ownership of raw materials and inputs& and government restrics such as licenses or patents. Network effects for certain products further increase the mopoly power that patents afford.
Because the demand curve faced by the mopolist is downward-sloping& the firm is a price setter. It will maximize profits by producing the quantity of output at which marginal cost equals marginal revenue. The profit-maximizing price is then found on the demand curve for that quantity.
Because a typical mopolist holds market price above marginal cost& the major impact of mopoly is a reduc in efficiency. Compared to a competitive market& the mopoly is characterized by more centralized power& potentially higher profits& and less pressure to be responsive to consumer preferences. Public policy toward mopoly includes antitrust laws and& in the case of natural mopolies& regula of price and other aspects of the firm’s behavior.

358 10.1 The Nature of Mopoly
Learning Objectives
Define mopoly and the relaship between price setting and mopoly power.
List and explain the sources of mopoly power and how they can change over time.
Define what is meant by a natural mopoly.
Mopoly is at the opposite end of the spectrum of market models from perfect competi. A mopoly firm has rivals. It is the only firm in its industry. There are close substitutes for the good or service a mopoly produces. t only does a mopoly firm have the market to itself& but it also need t worry about other firms entering. In the case of mopoly& entry by potential rivals is prohibitively difficult.
A mopoly does t take the market price as given; it determines its own price. It selects from its demand curve the price that corresponds to the quantity the firm has chosen to produce in order to earn the maximum profit possible. The entry of new firms& which eliminates profit in the long run in a competitive market& cant occur in the mopoly model.
A firm that sets or picks price based on its output decision is called a price setter. A firm that acts as a price setter possesses mopoly power. We shall see in the next chapter that mopolies are t the only firms that have price power; however& the absence of rivals in mopoly gives it much more price-setting power.
As was the case when we discussed perfect competi in the previous chapter& the assumps of the mopoly model are rather strong. In assuming there is one firm in a market& we assume there are other firms producing goods or services that could be considered part of the same market as that of the mopoly firm. In assuming blocked entry& we assume& for reasons we will discuss below& that other firm can enter that market. Such condis are rare in the real world. As always with models& we make the assumps that define mopoly in order to simplify our analysis& t to describe the real world. The result is a model that gives us important insights into the nature of the choices of firms and their impact on the ecomy.
Sources of Mopoly Power
Why are some markets dominated by single firms? What are the sources of mopoly power? Ecomists have identified a number of condis that& individually or in combina& can lead to domina of a market by a single firm and create barriers that prevent the entry of new firms.
Barriers to entry are characteristics of a particular market that block new firms from entering it. They include ecomies of scale& special advantages of loca& high sunk costs& a dominant posi in the ownership359 making entry that much more formidable. Although these barriers might allow one firm to gain and hold mopoly control over a market& there are often forces at work that can erode this control.
Ecomies of Scale
Scale ecomies and disectiomies define the shape of a firm’s long-run average cost (LRAC) curve as it increases its output. If long-run average cost declines as the level of produc increases& a firm is said to experience ecomies of scale.
A firm that confronts ecomies of scale over the entire range of outputs demanded in its industry is a natural mopoly. Utilities that distribute electricity& water& and natural gas to some markets are examples. In a natural mopoly& the LRAC of any one firm intersects the market demand curve where long-run average costs are falling or are at a minimum. If this is the case& one firm in the industry will expand to exploit the ecomies of scale available to it. Because this firm will have lower unit costs than its rivals& it can drive them out of the market and gain mopoly control over the industry.
Suppose there are 12 firms& each operating at the scale shown by ATC1 (average total cost) in figureure 10.1 “Ecomies of Scale Lead to Natural Mopoly”. A firm that expanded its scale of opera to achieve an average total cost curve such as ATC2 could produce 240 units of output at a lower cost than could the smaller firms producing 20 units each. By cutting its price below the minimum average total cost of the smaller plants& the larger firm could drive the smaller ones out of business. In this situa& the industry demand is t large eugh to support more than one firm. If ather firm attempted to enter the industry& the natural mopolist would always be able to undersell it.
figureure 10.1 Ecomies of Scale Lead to Natural Mopoly A firm with falling LRAC throughout the range of outputs relevant to existing demand (D) will mopolize the industry. Here& one360 at a smaller scale (ATC1)& and producing 20 units of output each.
Loca
Sometimes mopoly power is the result of loca. For example& sellers in markets isolated by distance from their nearest rivals have a degree of mopoly power. The local movie theater in a small town has a mopoly in showing first-run movies. Doctors& dentists& and mechanics in isolated towns may also be mopolists.
Sunk Costs
The greater the cost of establishing a new business in an industry& the more difficult it is to enter that industry. That cost will& in turn& be greater if the outlays required to start a business are unlikely to be recovered if the business should fail.
Suppose& for example& that entry into a particular industry requires extensive advertising to make consumers aware of the new brand. Should the effort fail& there is way to recover the expenditures for such advertising. An expenditure that has already been made and that cant be recovered is called a sunk cost.
If a substantial frac of a firm’s initial outlays will be lost upon exit from the industry& exit will be costly. Difficulty of exit can make for difficulty of entry. The more firms have to lose from an unsuccessful effort to penetrate a particular market& the less likely they are to try. The potential for high sunk costs could thus contribute to the mopoly power of an established firm by making entry by other firms more difficult.
Restricted Ownership of Raw Materials and Inputs
In very few cases the source of mopoly power is the ownership of strategic inputs. If a particular firm owns all of an input required for the produc of a particular good or service& then it could emerge as the only producer of that good or service.
The Aluminum Company of America (ALCOA) gained mopoly power through its ownership of virtually all the bauxite mines in the world (bauxite is the source of aluminum). The Internaal Nickel Company of Canada at one time owned virtually all the world’s nickel. De Beers acquired rights to nearly all the world’s diamond produc& giving it ermous power in the market for diamonds. With new diamond supplies in Canada& Australia& and Russia being developed and sold independently of DeBeers& however& this power has declined; today DeBeers controls a substantially smaller percentage of the world’s supply.
361 Government Restrics
Ather important basis for mopoly power consists of special privileges granted to some business firms by government agencies. State and local governments have commonly assigned exclusive franchises—rights to conduct business in a specific market—to taxi and bus companies& to cable television companies& and to providers of telephone services& electricity& natural gas& and water& although the trend in recent years has been to encourage competi for many of these services. Governments might also regulate entry into an industry or a profession through licensing and certifica requirements. Governments also provide patent protec to inventors of products or produc methods in order to encourage inva; these patents may afford their holders a degree of mopoly power during the 17-year life of the patent.
Patents can take on extra importance when network effects are present. Network effects arise in situas where products become more useful the larger the number of users of the product. For example& one advantage of using the Windows computer operating system is that so many other people use it. That has advantages in terms of sharing files and other informa.
Key Takeaways
An industry with a single firm& in which entry is blocked& is called a mopoly.
A firm that sets or picks price depending on its output decision is called a price setter. A price setter possesses mopoly power.
The sources of mopoly power include ecomies of scale& locaal advantages& high sunk costs associated with entry& restricted ownership of key inputs& and government restrics& such as exclusive franchises& licensing and certifica requirements& and patents.
A firm that confronts ecomies of scale over the entire range of output demanded in an industry is a natural mopoly.

This is t the world of perfect competi& where firms are indifferent about which firm has produced a particular product& where each firm kws it can sell all it wants at the going market price& where firms must settle for zero ecomic profit in the long run. r is it the world of mopoly& where a single firm maximizes its profits& believing that barriers to entry will keep out would-be competitors& at least for a while. This is the world of imperfect competi& one that lies between the idealized extremes of perfect competi and mopoly. It is a world in which firms battle over market shares& in which ecomic profits may persist& in which rivals try to outguess each other with pricing& advertising& and product development strategies.
Unlike the chapters on perfect competi and mopoly& this chapter does t provide a single model to explain firms’ behavior. There are too many varias on an uncertain theme for one model to explain the complexities of imperfect competi. Rather& the chapter provides an overview of some of the many different models and explanas advanced by ecomists for the behavior of firms in the imperfectly competitive marketplace. The analytical tools you have acquired in the course of studying the models of competitive and mopoly markets will be very much in evidence in this discussion.
The spectrum of business enterprise ranges from perfectly competitive firms to mopoly. Between these extremes lies the business landscape in which the vast majority of firms—those in the world of imperfect competi—actually operate. Imperfect competi is a market structure with more than one firm in an industry in which at least one firm is a price setter. An imperfectly competitive firm has a degree of mopoly power& either based on product differentia that leads to a downward-sloping demand curve or resulting from the interac of rival firms in an industry with only a few firms.
There are two broad categories of imperfectly competitive markets. The first is one in which many firms compete& each offering a slightly different product. The secd is one in which the industry is dominated by a few firms. Important features of both kinds of markets are advertising and price discrimina& which we examine later in this chapter. 366
11.1 Mopolistic Competi: Competi Among Many
Learning Objectives
Explain the main characteristics of a mopolistically competitive industry& describing both its similarities and differences from the models of perfect competi and mopoly.
Explain and illustrate both short-run equilibrium and long-run equilibrium for a mopolistically competitive firm.
Explain what it means to say that a firm operating under mopolistic competi has excess capacity in the long run and discuss the implicas of this conclusion.
The first model of an imperfectly competitive industry that we shall investigate has condis quite similar to those of perfect competi. The model of mopolistic competi assumes a large number of firms. It assumes easy entry and exit. This model differs from the model of perfect competi in one key respect: it assumes that the goods and services produced by firms are differentiated. This differentia may occur by virtue of advertising& convenience of loca& product quality& reputa of the seller& or other factors. Product differentia gives firms producing a particular product some degree of price-setting or mopoly power. However& because of the availability of close substitutes& the price-setting power of mopolistically competitive firms is quite limited. Mopolistic competi is a model characterized by many firms producing similar but differentiated products in a market with easy entry and exit.
Restaurants are a mopolistically competitive sector; in most areas there are many firms& each is differentiated& and entry and exit are very easy. Each restaurant has many close substitutes—these may include other restaurants& fast-food outlets& and the deli and frozen-food secs at local supermarkets. Other industries that exhibit mopolistic competi include retail stores& barber and beauty shops& auto-repair shops& service stas& law firms& and law and accounting firms.
Profit Maximiza
Suppose a restaurant raises its prices slightly above those of similar restaurants with which it competes. Will it have any customers? Probably. Because the restaurant is different from other restaurants& some people will continue to patronize it. Within limits& then& the restaurant can set its own prices; it does t take the market price as given. In fact& differentiated markets imply that the of a single “market price” is meaningless.
Because products in a mopolistically competitive industry are differentiated& firms face downward-sloping demand curves. Whenever a firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve& the graphical framework of mopoly can be used. In the short run& the model of mopolistic competi looks exactly like the model of mopoly. An important distinc between mopoly and mopolistic competi& however& emerges in the long run. We begin with an analysis of the short run.
367
The Short Run
Because a mopolistically competitive firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve& its marginal revenue curve is a downward-sloping line that lies below the demand curve& as in the mopoly model. We can thus use the model of mopoly that we have already developed to analyze the choices of a mopsony in the short run.
figureure 11.1 “Short-Run Equilibrium in Mopolistic Competi” shows the demand& marginal revenue& marginal cost& and average total cost curves facing a mopolistically competitive firm& Mama’s Pizza. Mama’s competes with several other similar firms in a market in which entry and exit are relatively easy. Mama’s demand curve D1 is downward-sloping; even if Mama’s raises its prices above those of its competitors& it will still have some customers. Given the downward-sloping demand curve& Mama’s marginal revenue curve MR1 lies below demand. To sell more pizzas& Mama’s must lower its price& and that means its marginal revenue from addial pizzas will be less than price.
figureure 11.1 Short-Run Equilibrium in Mopolistic Competi Looking at the intersec of the marginal revenue curve MR1 and the marginal cost curve MC& we see that the profit-maximizing quantity is 2&150 units per week. Reading up to the average total cost curve ATC& we see that the cost per unit equals $9.20. Price& given on the demand curve D1& is $10.40& so the profit per unit is $1.20. Total profit per week equals $1.20 times 2&150& or $2&580; it is shown by the shaded rectangle.
Given the marginal revenue curve MR and marginal cost curve MC& Mama’s will maximize profits by selling 2&150 pizzas per week. Mama’s demand curve tells us that it can sell that quantity at a price of $10.40. Looking at the average total cost curve ATC& we see that the firm’s cost per unit is $9.20. Its ecomic profit per unit is thus $1.20. Total ecomic profit& shown by the shaded rectangle& is $2&580 per week. 368
The Long Run
We see in figureure 11.1 “Short-Run Equilibrium in Mopolistic Competi” that Mama’s Pizza is earning an ecomic profit. If Mama’s experience is typical& then other firms in the market are also earning returns that exceed what their owners could be earning in some related activity. Positive ecomic profits will encourage new firms to enter Mama’s market.
As new firms enter& the availability of substitutes for Mama’s pizzas will increase& which will reduce the demand facing Mama’s Pizza and make the demand curve for Mama’s Pizza more elastic. Its demand curve will shift to the left. Any shift in a demand curve shifts the marginal revenue curve as well. New firms will continue to enter& shifting the demand curves for existing firms to the left& until pizza firms such as Mama’s longer make an ecomic profit. The zero-profit solu occurs where Mama’s demand curve is tangent to its average total cost curve—at point A in figureure 11.2 “Mopolistic Competi in the Long Run”. Mama’s price will fall to $10 per pizza and its output will fall to 2&000 pizzas per week. Mama’s will just cover its opportunity costs& and thus earn zero ecomic profit. At any other price& the firm’s cost per unit would be greater than the price at which a pizza could be sold& and the firm would sustain an ecomic loss. Thus& the firm and the industry are in long-run equilibrium. There is incentive for firms to either enter or leave the industry.
figureure 11.2 Mopolistic Competi in the Long Run The existence of ecomic profits in a mopolistically competitive industry will induce entry in the long run. As new firms enter& the demand curve D1 and marginal revenue curve MR1 facing a typical firm will shift to the left& to D2 and MR2. Eventually& this shift produces a profit-maximizing solu at zero ecomic profit& where D2 is tangent to the average total cost curve ATC (point A). The long-run equilibrium solu here is an output of 2&000 units per week at a price of $10 per unit.
Had Mama’s Pizza and other similar restaurants been incurring ecomic losses& the process of moving to long-run equilibrium would work in reverse. Some firms would exit. With fewer substitutes available& the demand curve faced by each remaining firm would shift to the right. Price and output at each restaurant would rise. Exit would continue until the industry was in long-run equilibrium& with the typical firm earning zero ecomic profit.
Such comings and goings are typical of mopolistic competi. Because entry and exit are easy& favorable369 profit opportunities attract new rivals& and unprofitable industries lose firms until the survivors are making zero ecomic profit. But the model of mopolistic competi assumes that barriers to entry are low& so the long-run equilibrium will always drive ecomic profits to zero.
Mama’s Pizza is t likely to take these threats lying down. It will seek ways to maintain its ecomic profit. It may attempt to improve the quality of its product or service. It might launch advertising campaigns to attract customers. Mama’s may change its hours or offerings. All these efforts& however& are costly. Other firms in the market can be expected to try similar strategies& thus competing away any ecomic profit.
Suppose Mama’s introduces a new pizza that attracts new customers and creates ecomic profit again. This above-rmal profit is once again a signal to other firms. Some will copy the inva; others will try to come up with something different and better. The process of competing for ecomic profits is a constant process in mopolistic competi. For a firm to earn ecomic profit& it must find ways to distinguish itself from its rivals. When it does& rivals will try to copy whatever gave the firm its edge. Often it will be difficult for any firm to maintain ecomic profit in the long run.
The key thing to te is that in the kind of scenario described above—where Mama’s has attracted customers with a new& popular pizza—ecomic profits are possible in the short run. To compete successfully& rivals will need to come up with just the right product to pull customers and profits away from Mama’s. But as long as Mama’s continues to earn ecomic profits& there will be incentives for other firms to try.
Heads Up!
The term “mopolistic competi” is easy to confuse with the term “mopoly.” Remember& however& that the two models are characterized by quite different market condis. A mopoly is a single firm with high barriers to entry. Mopolistic competi implies an industry with many firms& differentiated products& and easy entry and exit.
Why is the term mopolistic competi used to describe this type of market structure? The reason is that it bears some similarities to both perfect competi and to mopoly. Mopolistic competi is similar to perfect competi in that in both of these market structures many firms make up the industry and entry and exit are fairly easy. Mopolistic competi is similar to mopoly in that& like mopoly firms& mopolistically competitive firms have at least some discre when it comes to setting prices. However& because mopolistically competitive firms produce goods that are close substitutes for those of rival firms& the degree of mopoly power that mopolistically competitive firms possess is very low.
Excess Capacity: The Price of Variety
The long-run equilibrium solu in mopolistic competi always produces zero ecomic profit at a point to the left of the minimum of the average total cost curve. That is because the zero profit solu occurs at the point where the downward-sloping demand curve is tangent to the average total cost curve& and thus the average total cost curve is itself downward-sloping. By expanding output& the firm could lower average total cost. The firm thus produces less than the output at which it would minimize average total cost. A firm that operates to the left of the lowest point on its average total cost curve has excess capacity.
Because mopolistically competitive firms charge prices that exceed marginal cost& mopolistic competi is inefficient. The marginal benefit consumers receive from an addial unit of the good is given by its price. Since the benefit of an addial unit of output is greater than the marginal cost& consumers would be better off if output were expanded. Furthermore& an expansion of output would reduce average total cost. But mopolistically competitive firms will t voluntarily increase output& since for them& the marginal revenue would be less than the marginal cost.
One can thus criticize a mopolistically competitive industry for falling short of the efficiency standard of perfect competi. But mopolistic competi is inefficient because of product differentia. Think of a mopolistically competitive activity in your area. Would consumers be better off if all the firms in this industry produced identical products so that they could match the assumps of perfect competi? If identical products were impossible& would consumers be better off if some of the firms were ordered to shut down on grounds that the model predicts there will be “too many” firms? The inefficiency of mopolistic competi may be a small price to pay for a wide range of product choices. Furthermore& remember that perfect competi is merely a model; it is t a goal toward which an ecomy might strive as an alternative to mopolistic competi.
370
Key Takeaways
A mopolistically competitive industry features some of the same characteristics as perfect competi: a large number of firms and easy entry and exit.
The characteristic that distinguishes mopolistic competi from perfect competi is differentiated products; each firm is a price setter and thus faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
Short-run equilibrium for a mopolistically competitive firm is identical to that of a mopoly firm. The firm produces an output at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost and sets its price according to its demand curve.
In the long run in mopolistic competi any ecomic profits or losses will be eliminated by entry or exit& leaving firms with zero ecomic profit.
A mopolistically competitive industry will have some excess capacity; this may be viewed as the cost of the product diversity that this market structure produces.

11.2 Oligopoly: Competi Among the Few
Learning Objectives
Explain the main characteristics of an oligopoly& differentiating it from other types of market structures.
Explain the measures that are used to determine the degree of concentra in an industry.
Explain and illustrate the collusion model of oligopoly.
Discuss how game theory can be used to understand the behavior of firms in an oligopoly.
In July& 2005& General Motors Corpora (GMC) offered “employee discount pricing” to virtually all its customers& t just employees and their relatives. This new marketing strategy introduced by GMC obviously affected Ford& Chrysler& Toyota and other automobile and truck manufacturers; Ford matched GMC’s employee discount plan by offering up to $1&000 to its own employees who convinced friends to purchase its cars and trucks. Ford also offered its customers the same prices paid by its employees. By mid-July& Chrysler indicated that it was looking at many alternatives& but was waiting for GMC to make its next move. Ultimately& Chrysler also offered employee discount pricing.
Toyota had to respond. It quickly developed a new marketing strategy of its own& which included lowering the prices of its cars and offering new financing terms. The responses of Ford& Chrysler& and Toyota to GMC’s new strategy obviously affected the outcome of that strategy. Similarly& a decision by Procter & Gamble to lower the price of Crest toothpaste may elicit a response from Colgate-Palmolive& and that response will affect the success of Crest. In an oligopoly& the fourth and final market structure that we will study& the market is dominated by a few firms& each of which recognizes that its own acs will produce a response from its rivals and that these responses will affect it.
The firms that dominate an oligopoly recognize that they are interdependent: What one firm does affects each of the others. This interdependence stands in sharp contrast to the models of perfect competi and mopolistic competi& where we assume that each firm is so small that it assumes the rest of the market will& in effect& igre what it does. A perfectly competitive firm responds to the market& t to the acs of any other firm. A mopolistically competitive firm responds to its own demand& t to the acs of specific rivals. These presumps greatly simplify the analysis of perfect competi and mopolistic competi. We do t have that luxury in oligopoly& where the interdependence of firms is the defining characteristic of the market.
Some oligopoly industries make standardized products: steel& aluminum& wire& and industrial tools. Others make differentiated products: cigarettes& automobiles& computers& ready-to-eat breakfast cereal& and soft drinks. 375
Measuring Concentra in Oligopoly
Oligopoly means that a few firms dominate an industry. But how many is “a few&” and how large a share of industry output does it take to “dominate” the industry?
Compare& for example& the ready-to-eat breakfast cereal industry and the ice cream industry. The cereal industry is dominated by two firms& Kellogg’s and General Mills& which together hold more than half the cereal market. This oligopoly operates in a highly concentrated market. The market for ice cream& where the four largest firms account for just less than a third of output& is much less concentrated.
One way to measure the degree to which output in an industry is concentrated among a few firms is the concentra ratio& which reports the percentage of output accounted for by the largest firms in an industry. The higher the concentra ratio& the more the firms in the industry take account of their rivals’ behavior. The lower the concentra ratio& the more the industry reflects the characteristics of mopolistic competi or perfect competi.
The U.S. Census Bureau& based on surveys it conducts of manufacturing firms every five years& reports concentra ratios. These surveys show concentra ratios for the largest 4& 8& 20& and 50 firms in each industry category. Some concentra ratios from the 2002 survey& the latest available& are reported in Table 11.1 “Concentra Ratios and Herfindahl–Hirschman Indexes”. tice that the four-firm concentra ratio for breakfast cereals is 78%; for ice cream it is 48%.

An alternative measure of concentra is found by squaring the percentage share (stated as a whole number) of each firm in an industry and then summing these squares. This measure is called the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index376 (HHI). The largest HHI possible is the case of mopoly& where one firm has 100% of the market; the index equals 1002& or 10&000.
