Suppose the mopsony firm is w using three units of the factor at a price of $6 per unit. Its total factor cost is $18. Suppose the firm is considering adding one more unit of the factor. Given the supply curve& the only way the firm can obtain four units of the factor rather than three is to offer a higher price of $8 for all four units of the factor. That would increase the firm’s total factor cost from $18 to $32. The marginal factor cost of the fourth unit of the factor is thus $14. It includes the $8 the firm pays for the fourth unit plus an addial $2 for each of the three units the firm was already using& since it has increased the prices for the factor to $8 from $6. The marginal factor cost (MFC) exceeds the price of the factor. We can plot the MFC for each increase in the quantity of the factor the firm uses; tice in figureure 14.2 “Supply and Marginal Factor Cost” that the MFC curve lies above the supply curve. As always in plotting in marginal values& we plot the $14 midway between units three and four because it is the increase in factor cost as the firm goes from three to four units.
Mopsony Equilibrium and the Marginal Decision Rule
The marginal decision rule& as it applies to a firm’s use of factors& calls for the firm to add more units of a factor up to the point that the factor’s MRP is equal to its MFC. figureure 14.3 “Mopsony Equilibrium” illustrates the solu for a firm that is the only buyer of labor in a particular market.
figureure 14.3 Given the supply curve for labor& S& and the marginal factor cost curve& MFC& the mopsony firm will select the quantity of labor at which the MRP of labor equals its MFC. It thus uses Lm units of labor (determined by at the intersec of MRP and MFC) and pays a wage of Wm per unit (the wage is taken from the supply curve at which Lm units of labor are available). The quantity of labor used by the mopsony firm is less than would be used in a competitive market (Lc); the wage paid& Wm& is lower than would be paid in a competitive labor market.
475
The firm faces the supply curve for labor& S& and the marginal factor cost curve for labor& MFC. The profit-maximizing quantity is determined by the intersec of the MRP and MFC curves—the firm will hire Lm units of labor. The wage at which the firm can obtain Lm units of labor is given by the supply curve for labor; it is Wm. Labor receives a wage that is less than its MRP.
If the mopsony firm was broken up into a large number of small firms and all other condis in the market remained unchanged& then the sum of the MRP curves for individual firms would be the market demand for labor. The equilibrium wage would be Wc& and the quantity of labor demanded would be Lc. Thus& compared to a competitive market& a mopsony solu generates a lower factor price and a smaller quantity of the factor demanded.
Mopoly and Mopsony: A Comparison 476
There is a close relaship between the models of mopoly and mopsony. A clear understanding of this relaship will help to clarify both models.
figureure 14.4 “Mopoly and Mopsony” compares the mopoly and mopsony equilibrium solus. Both types of firms are price setters: The mopoly is a price setter in its product market; the mopsony is a price setter in its factor market. Both firms must change price to change quantity: The mopoly must lower its product price to sell an addial unit of output& and the mopsony must pay more to hire an addial unit of the factor. Because both types of firms must adjust prices to change quantities& the marginal consequences of their choices are t given by the prices they charge (for products) or pay (for factors). For a mopoly& marginal revenue is less than price; for a mopsony& marginal factor cost is greater than price.
figureure 14.4 The graphs and the table provide a comparison of mopoly and mopsony.
Market Choice Mopoly Mopsony
Nature of pricing choice Price setter in product market. Price setter in factor market.
Marginal consequences of choices Selling an addial unit generates marginal revenue MR& which is less than product price. Using an addial unit generates marginal factor cost MFC& which is greater than factor price.
Profit-maximizing solu Produce where MR equals marginal cost MC—Qm in Panel (a). Use the factor at the quantity where MRP equals MFC—FQm in Panel (b).
Price Determined by the point on the demand curve D that corresponds to the profit-maximizing quantity of product—Pm in Panel (a). Determined by the point on the supply curve that corresponds to the profit-maximizing quantity of the factor—FPm in Panel (b).
Both types of firms follow the marginal decision rule: A mopoly produces a quantity of the product at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost; a mopsony employs a quantity of the factor at which marginal revenue product equals marginal factor cost. Both firms set prices at which they can sell or purchase the profit-maximizing quantity. The mopoly sets its product price based on the demand curve it faces; the mopsony sets its factor price based on the factor supply curve it faces.
Mopsony in the Real World 477
Although cases of pure mopsony are rare& there are many situas in which buyers have a degree of mopsony power. A buyer has mopsony power if it faces an upward-sloping supply curve for a good& service& or factor of produc.
For example& a firm that accounts for a large share of employment in a small community may be large eugh relative to the labor market that it is t a price taker. Instead& it must raise wages to attract more workers and thus faces an upward-sloping supply curve and has mopsony power. Because buyers are more likely to have mopsony power in factor markets than in product markets& we shall focus on those.
The next sec examines mopsony power in professional sports.
Mopsonies in Sports
Professional sports provide a setting in which ecomists can test theories of wage determina in competitive versus mopsony labor markets. In their analyses& ecomists assume professional teams are profit-maximizing firms that hire labor (athletes and other workers) to produce a product: entertainment bought by the fans who watch their games and by other firms that sponsor the games. Fans influence revenues directly by purchasing tickets and indirectly by generating the ratings that determine television and radio advertising revenues from broadcasts of games.
In a competitive system& a player should receive a wage equal to his or her MRP—the increase in team revenues the player is able to produce. As New York Yankees owner George Steinbrenner once put it& “You measure the value of a ballplayer by how many fannies he puts in the seats.”
The mopsony model& however& predicts that players facing mopsony employers will receive wages far less than their MRPs. A test of mopsony theory& then& would be to determine whether players in competitive markets receive wages equal to their MRPs and whether players in mopsony markets receive less.
Since the late 1970s& there has been a major shift in the rules that govern relas between professional athletes and owners of sports teams. The shift has turned the once mopsonistic market for professional athletes into a competitive one. Before 1977& for example& professional baseball players in the United States played under the terms of the “reserve clause&” which specified that a player was “owned” by his team. Once a team had acquired a player’s contract& the team could sell& trade& retain& or dismiss the player. Unless the team dismissed him& the player was unable to offer his services for competitive bidding by other teams. Moreover& players entered major league baseball through a draft that was structured so that only one team had the right to bid for any one player. Throughout a player’s career& then& there was always only one team that could bid on him—each player faced a mopsony purchaser for his services to major league baseball.
Condis were similar in other professional sports. Many studies have shown that the salaries of professional athletes in various team sports fell far short of their MRPs while mopsony prevailed.
players could offer their services to other teams& owners began to bid for their services. Profit-maximizing firms were willing to pay athletes their MRPs. Average annual salaries for baseball players rose from about $51&000 in 1975 to nearly $1.4 million in 1997. Average annual player salaries in men’s basketball rose from $109&000 in 1976 to $2.24 million in 1998. Football players worked under an almost pure form of mopsony until 1993& when a few players were allowed free agency status each year. In 1993& when 484 players were released to the market as free agents& those players received pay increases averaging more than 100%. Under the NFL collective bargaining agreement in effect in 1998& players could become unrestricted free agents if they had been playing for four years. There were 305 unrestricted free agents (out of a total player pool of approximately 1&700) that year. About half signed new contracts with their old teams while the other half signed with new teams. Given the dramatic impact on player salaries of more competitive markets for athletes& events such as the 2004–2005 lockout in hockey came as surprise. The agreement between the owners of hockey teams and players in 2005 to limit the total payroll of each team reinstates some of the old mopsony power of the owners. Players had a huge financial stake in resisting such attempts.
Mopsony in Other Labor Markets
A firm that has a dominant posi in a local labor market may have mopsony power in that market. Even if a firm does t dominate the total labor market& it may have mopsony power over certain types of labor. For example& a hospital may be the only large employer of nurses in a local market& and it may have mopsony power in employing them.
Colleges and universities generally pay part-time instructors considerably less for teaching a particular course than they pay full-time instructors. In part& the difference reflects the fact that full-time faculty members are expected to do research and perform other duties. But mopsony may provide an addial explana.
Part-time instructors are likely to have other regular employment. A university hiring a local accountant to teach a sec of accounting does t have to worry that that person will go to ather state to find a better offer for part-time instructor. For part-time teaching& then& the university may be the only employer in town—and thus able to exert mopsony power to drive the part-time instructor’s wage below the instructor’s MRP. 479
Mopsony in Other Factor Markets
Mopsony power may also exist in markets for factors other than labor. The military in different countries& for example& has considerable mopsony power in the market for sophisticated military goods. Major retailers may have some mopsony power with respect to some of their suppliers. Sears& for example& is the only wholesale buyer of Craftsman brand tools. One major development in medical care in recent years has been the emergence of managed care organizas that contract with a large number of employers to purchase medical services on behalf of employees. These organizas often have sufficient mopsony power to force down the prices charged by providers such as drug companies& physicians& and hospitals. Countries in which health care is provided by the government& such as Canada and the United Kingdom& are able to exert mopsony power in their purchases of health care services.
Whatever the source of mopsony power& the expected result is the same. Buyers with mopsony power are likely to pay a lower price and to buy a smaller quantity of a particular factor than buyers who operate in a competitive environment.
Key Takeaways
In the mopsony model there is one buyer for a good& service& or factor of produc. A mopsony firm is a price setter in the market in which it has mopsony power.
The mopsony buyer selects a profit-maximizing solu by employing the quantity of factor at which marginal factor cost (MFC) equals marginal revenue product (MRP) and paying the price on the factor’s supply curve corresponding to that quantity.
A degree of mopsony power exists whenever a firm faces an upward-sloping supply curve for a factor.

Case in Point: Professional Player Salaries and Mopsony
figureure 14.7 Brian Moran – Opening Weekend At Oriole Park – CC BY-NC 2.0.
481
Professional athletes have t always enjoyed the freedom they have today to seek better offers from other teams. Before 1977& for example& baseball players could deal only with the team that owned their contract—one that “reserved” the player to that team. This reserve clause gave teams mopsony power over the players they employed. Similar restrics hampered player mobility in men’s football& basketball& and hockey.
Gerald Scully& an ecomist at the University of Texas at Dallas& estimated the impact of the reserve clause on baseball player salaries. He sought to demonstrate that the player salaries fell short of MRP. Mr. Scully estimated the MRP of players in a two-step process. First& he studied the determinants of team attendance. He found that in addi to factors such as popula and income in a team’s home city& the team’s win-loss record had a strong effect on attendance. secd& he examined the player characteristics that determined win-loss records. He found that for hitters& batting average was the variable most closely associated with a team’s winning percentage. For pitchers& it was the earned-run average—the number of earned runs allowed by a pitcher per nine innings pitched.
With equas that predicted a team’s attendance and its win-loss record& Mr. Scully was able to take a particular player& describe him by his statistics& and compute his MRP. Mr. Scully then subtracted costs associated with each player for such things as transporta& lodging& meals& and uniforms to obtain the player’s net MRP. He then compared players’ net MRPs to their salaries.
Mr. Scully’s results& displayed in the table below& show net MRP and salaries& estimated on a career basis& for players he classified as mediocre& average& and star-quality& based on their individual statistics. For average and star-quality players& salaries fell far below net MRP& just as the theory of mopsony suggests. 482

The fact that mediocre players with negative net MRPs received salaries presents something of a puzzle. One explana could be that when they were signed to contracts& these players were expected to perform well& so their salaries reflected their expected contribus to team revenues. Their actual performance fell short& so their wages exceeded their MRP. Ather explana could be that teams paid young players more than they were expected to contribute to revenues early in their careers in hopes that they would develop into profitable members of the team. In any event& Mr. Scully found that the costs of mediocre players exceeded their estimated contribu to team revenues& giving them negative net MRPs.
In 1977& a lawsuit filed by several baseball players resulted in the partial dismantling of the reserve clause. 14.2 486 Mopsony and the Minimum Wage
Learning Objectives
Compare the impact of a minimum wage on employment in the case where the labor market is perfectly competitive to the case of a mopsony labor market.
Discuss the debate among ecomists concerning the impact of raising the minimum wage.
We have seen that wages will be lower in mopsony than in otherwise similar competitive labor markets. In a competitive market& workers receive wages equal to their MRPs. Workers employed by mopsony firms receive wages that are less than their MRPs. This fact suggests sharply different conclusions for the analysis of minimum wages in competitive versus mopsony condis.
In a competitive market& the imposi of a minimum wage above the equilibrium wage necessarily reduces employment& as we learned in the chapter on perfectly competitive labor markets. In a mopsony market& however& a minimum wage above the equilibrium wage could increase employment at the same time as it raises wages!
figureure 14.9 “Minimum Wage and Mopsony” shows a mopsony employer that faces a supply curve& from which we derive the marginal factor cost curve& MFC. The firm maximizes profit by employing Lm units of labor and paying a wage of $4 per hour. The wage is below the firm’s MRP.
figureure 14.9 A mopsony employer faces a supply curve S& a marginal factor cost curve MFC& and a marginal revenue product curve MRP. It maximizes profit by employing Lm units of labor and paying a wage of $4 per hour. The imposi of a minimum wage of $5 per hour makes the dashed secs of the supply and MFC curves irrelevant. The marginal factor cost curve is thus a horizontal line at $5 up to L1 units of labor. MRP and MFC w intersect at L2 so that employment increases.
487
w suppose the government imposes a minimum wage of $5 per hour; it is illegal for firms to pay less. At this minimum wage& L1 units of labor are supplied. To obtain any smaller quantity of labor& the firm must pay the minimum wage. That means that the sec of the supply curve showing quantities of labor supplied at wages below $5 is irrelevant; the firm cant pay those wages. tice that the sec of the supply curve below $5 is shown as a dashed line. If the firm wants to hire more than L1 units of labor& however& it must pay wages given by the supply curve.
Marginal factor cost is affected by the minimum wage. To hire addial units of labor up to L1& the firm pays the minimum wage. The addial cost of labor beyond L1 continues to be given by the original MFC curve. The MFC curve thus has two segments: a horizontal segment at the minimum wage for quantities up to L1 and the solid por of the MFC curve for quantities beyond that.
The firm will still employ labor up to the point that MFC equals MRP. In the case shown in figureure 14.9 “Minimum Wage and Mopsony”& that occurs at L2. The firm thus increases its employment of labor in response to the minimum wage. This theoretical conclusion received apparent empirical valida in a study by David Card and Alan Krueger of employment in the fast food industry. 488That conclusion became an important political tool for proponents of an increase in the minimum wage. The validity of those results has come under serious challenge& however& and the basic conclusion that a higher minimum wage would increase unemployment among unskilled workers in most cases remains the posi of most ecomists. The discussion in the Case in Point summarizes the debate.
Key Takeaways
In a competitive labor market& an increase in the minimum wage reduces employment and increases unemployment.
A minimum wage could increase employment in a mopsony labor market at the same time it increases wages.
Some ecomists argue that the mopsony model characterizes all labor markets and that this justifies a naal increase in the minimum wage.
Most ecomists argue that a nawide increase in the minimum wage would reduce employment among low-wage workers.
Try It!
Using the data in te 14.5 “Try It!”& suppose a minimum wage of $40 per day is imposed. How will this affect the firm’s use of labor?
Case in Point: The Mopsony-Minimum Wage Controversy
figureure 14.10 Annette Bernhardt – Fast Food Strikes& NYC& July 2013 – CC BY-SA 2.0.
489
While the imposi of a minimum wage on a mopsony employer could increase employment and wages at the same time& the possibility is generally regarded as empirically unimportant& given the rarity of cases of mopsony power in labor markets. However& some studies have found that increases in the minimum wage have led to either increased employment or to significant reducs in employment. These results appear to contradict the competitive model of demand and supply in the labor market& which predicts that an increase in the minimum wage will lead to a reduc in employment and an increase in unemployment.
The study that sparked the controversy was an analysis by David Card and Alan Krueger of employment in the fast food industry in Pennsylvania and New Jersey. New Jersey increased its minimum wage to $5.05 per hour in 1992& when 490the naal minimum wage was $4.25 per hour. The two ecomists surveyed 410 fast food restaurants in the Burger King& KFC& Roy Rogers& and Wendy’s chains just before New Jersey increased its minimum and again 10 months after the increase.
There was statistically significant change in employment in the New Jersey franchises& but employment fell in the Pennsylvania franchises. Thus& employment in the New Jersey franchises “rose” relative to employment in the Pennsylvania franchises. Card and Krueger’s results were widely interpreted as showing an increase in employment in New Jersey as a result of the increase in the minimum wage there.
Do minimum wages reduce employment or t? Some ecomists interpreted the Card and Krueger results as demonstrating widespread mopsony power in the labor market. Ecomist Alan Manning tes that the competitive model implies that a firm that pays a penny less than the market equilibrium wage will have zero employees. Mr. Manning tes that there are n-wage attributes to any job that& together with the cost of changing jobs& result in individual employers facing upward-sloping supply curves for labor and thus giving them mopsony power. And& as we have seen& a firm with mopsony power may respond to an increase in the minimum wage by increasing employment.
The difficulty with implementing this conclusion on a naal basis is that& even if firms do have a degree of mopsony power& it is impossible to determine just how much power any one firm has and by how much the minimum wage should be increased for each firm. As a result& even if it were true that firms had such mopsony power& it would t follow that an increase in the minimum wage would be appropriate.
Even the finding that an increase in the minimum wage may t reduce employment has been called into ques. There are many empirical studies that suggest that increases in the minimum wage do reduce employment. For example& a recent study of employment in the restaurant industry by Chicago Federal Reserve Bank ecomists Daniel Aaronson and Eric French concluded that a 10% increase in the minimum wage would reduce employment among unskilled restaurant workers by 2 to 4%. This finding was more in line with other empirical work. Further& ecomists point out that jobs have nwage elements. Hours of work& working condis& fellow employees& health insurance& and other fringe benefits of working can all be adjusted by firms in response to an increase in the minimum wage. Dwight Lee& an ecomist at the University of Georgia& argues that as a result& an increase in the minimum wage may t reduce employment but may reduce other fringe benefits that workers value more highly than wages themselves. So& an increase in the minimum wage may make even workers who receive higher wages worse off. One indicator that suggests that higher minimum wages may reduce the welfare of low income workers is that participa in the labor force by teenagers has been shown to fall as a result of higher minimum wages. If the opportunity to earn higher wages reduces the number of teenagers seeking those wages& it may indicate that low-wage work has become less desirable.
In short& the possibility that higher minimum wages might t reduce employment among low-wage workers does t necessarily mean that higher minimum wages improve the welfare of low income workers. Evidence that casts doubt on the proposi that higher minimum wages reduce employment does t remove many ecomists’ doubt that higher minimum wages would be a good policy. Lee& “The Minimum Wage Can Harm Workers by Reducing Unemployment&” Journal of Labor Research& 25(4) (Fall 2004); Andrew Leigh& “Employment Effects of Minimum Wages: Evidence from a Quasi-Experiment&” The Australian Ecomic Review& 36 (2003): 361–73; Andrew Leigh& “Employment Effects of Minimum Wages: Evidence from a Quasi-Experiment—Erratum&” The Australian Ecomic Review& 37(1): 102–5; Alan Manning& “Mopsony and the Efficiency of Labour Market Intervens&” Labour Ecomics& 11(2) (April 2004): 145–63; Walter J. 14.3 492 Price Setters on the Supply Side
Learning Objectives
Explain and illustrate how a mopoly supplier of some factor of produc maximizes profit.
Discuss some of the ways that labor unions try to exercise market power.
Define bilateral mopoly and explain and illustrate why prices in the model are indeterminate.
Explain how professional associas and producers’ cooperatives affect supply.
Buyers are t the only agents capable of exercising market power in factor-pricing choices. Suppliers of goods and services can exercise market power and act as price setters themselves in two ways. First& a supplier may have a mopoly or have a degree of mopoly power in the supply of a factor. In that case& ecomists analyze the firm’s choices as they would analyze those of any other imperfectly competitive firm. secd& individual suppliers of a factor of produc may band together in an associa to gain clout in the marketplace. Farmers& for example& often join forces to offset what they perceive as unfair market power on the part of buyers of their products. Workers may join together in a union in order to enhance their bargaining power with their employers. Each case is discussed below.
Mopoly Suppliers
A firm with mopoly power over a particular factor can be expected to behave like any other mopoly firm—choose its output where the marginal revenue and marginal cost curves intersect and charge a price taken from the demand curve.
figureure 14.11 A mopoly supplier of a factor of produc acts just as any other mopoly firm. Here& the mopoly faces the demand curve D and the marginal revenue curve MR. Given the marginal cost curve MC& it maximizes profit by supplying Qm and charging a price Pm.
493
A mopoly supplier of a factor faces a demand curve that represents the MRP of the factor. This situa is illustrated in figureure 14.11 “Mopoly Factor Supply”. The firm will charge a price Pm equal to the MRP of the factor and sell Qm units of the factor.
Unions
Workers in a competitive market receive a wage equal to their MRP. If they face mopsony power& they get less. Regardless of the market structure& workers are likely to seek higher wages and better working condis. One way they can try to improve their ecomic status is to organize into a labor union& an associa of workers that seeks to raise wages and to improve working condis. Unions represent their members in collective bargaining& a process of negotia of worker contracts between unions and employers. To strengthen its posi& a union may threaten a strike—a refusal by union members to work—unless its demands are met.
A Brief History of Unions 494
Workers have united to try to better their lot at least since the Middle Ages& when the first professional guilds were formed in Europe. In the United States& “workingmen’s societies” sprang up in the late eighteenth century. These organizas were craft unions uniting skilled workers in the same trade in an attempt to increase wages& shorten working hours& and regulate working condis for their members.
One goal unions consistently sought was a closed shop& where only union members can be hired—an arrangement that gives unions mopoly power in the supply of labor. A secd objective was to gain greater political and ecomic strength by joining together associas of different crafts. Union goals went largely unfulfilled until the twentieth century& when the courts began to favor collective bargaining between workers and employers in disputes over wages and working condis. Closed-shop arrangements are illegal in the United States today& but many states permit union shop arrangements& in which a firm is allowed to hire nunion workers who are required to join the union within a specified period. About 20 states have right-to-work laws which prohibit union shop rules.
The development of the industrial union& a form of union that represents the employees of a particular industry regardless of their craft& also aided the growth of the labor movement. The largest industrial union in the United States& the AFL-CIO& was formed in 1955& when unions accounted for just over 35% of the labor force. The AFL-CIO remains an important ecomic and political force& but union strength has fallen since its peak in the 1950s; today& less than 10% of workers in the private sector belong to unions. Quite dramatically& in 2005& three unions representing about a third of the total membership& withdrew from the AFL-CIO. The break-away unions argued that they would be more successful working on their own to recruit new members. The impact of this break will t be kwn for several years.
Part of the reason for the failure of unions to represent a larger share of workers lies in the market forces that govern wages. As the marginal revenue product of workers has risen throughout the ecomy& their wages have increased as well—whether they belonged to a union or t. Impressive ecomy-wide wage gains over the past two centuries may be one reason why the attrac of unions has remained weak.
Higher Wages and Other Union Goals
Higher wages once dominated the list of union objectives& but more recent agreements have also focused on nwage issues involving job security& health insurance& provision of child care& and job safety. Unions such as the United Auto Workers have negotiated contracts under which members who are laid off will continue to receive payments nearly equal to the wages they earned while on the job. They have also pushed hard for retirement pensions and for greater worker involvement in management decisions.
Union efforts to obtain higher wages have different effects on workers depending on the nature of the labor market. When unions confront an employer with mopsony power& their task is clear: they seek a wage closer to MRP than the employer is paying. If the labor market is a competitive one in which wages are determined by demand and supply& the union’s task is more difficult. Increasing the wage requires either increasing the demand 495for labor or reducing its supply. If unions succeed in increasing demand or a reduc in supply& then the higher wage will create a surplus of labor& or unemployment.
Increasing Demand
The demand for labor in a competitive market is found by summing the MRP curves of individual firms. Increasing demand thus requires increasing the marginal product of labor or raising the price of the good produced by labor.
One way that unions can increase the marginal product of their members is by encouraging investment in human capital. Consequently& unions may pressure firms to implement training programs. Some unions conduct training efforts themselves.
Ather way to increase the MRP of a factor is to reduce the use by firms of substitute factors. Unions generally represent skilled workers& and they are vigorous proponents of minimum wage laws that make unskilled workers more expensive. A higher minimum wage induces firms to substitute skilled for unskilled labor and thus increases the demand for the skilled workers unions represent.
Still ather way to increase the MRP of labor is to increase the demand for the products labor produces. The form this union activity generally takes is in the promo of “Made in the U.S.A.” goods. Unions have also promoted restrictive trade legisla aimed at reducing the supply of foreign goods and thus increasing the demand for domestic ones.
Reducing Labor Supply
Unions can restrict the supply of labor in two ways. First& they can seek to slow the growth of the labor force; unions from the earliest times have aggressively opposed immigra. Union support for Social security also reduces the labor supply by encouraging workers to retire early. secd& unions can promote policies that make it difficult for workers to enter a particular craft. Unions representing plumbers and electrical workers& for example& have restricted the number of people who can enter these crafts in some areas by requiring that workers belong to the union and then limiting the union’s membership.
Bilateral Mopoly
Suppose a union has negotiated a closed-shop arrangement (in a country where such arrangements are legal) with an employer that possesses mopsony power in its labor market. The union has a kind of mopoly in the supply of labor. A situa in which a mopsony buyer faces a mopoly seller is called bilateral mopoly. Prices in this model are indeterminate& with the actual wage falling somewhere between the pure mopoly and pure mopsony outcomes.
figureure 14.12 If the union has mopoly power over the supply of labor and faces a mopsony purchaser of the labor the union represents& the wage negotiated between the two will be indeterminate. The employer will hire Lm units of the labor per period. The employer wants a wage Wm on the supply curve S. The union will seek a wage close to the maximum the employer would be willing to pay for this quantity& Wu& at the intersec of the marginal revenue product (MRP) and the marginal factor cost (MFC) curves. The actual wage will be somewhere between these two amounts.
496
figureure 14.12 “Bilateral Mopoly” shows the same mopsony situa in a labor market that was shown in figureure 14.3 “Mopsony Equilibrium”. The employer will seek to pay a wage Wm for a quantity of labor Lm. The union will seek Wu& the highest wage the employer would be willing to pay for that quantity of labor. This wage is found on the MRP curve. The model of bilateral mopoly does t tell us the wage that will emerge. Whether the final wage will be closer to what the union seeks or closer to what the employer seeks will depend on the bargaining strength of the union and of the employer.
Unions and the Ecomy: An Assessment
Where unions operate effectively in otherwise competitive markets& they may reduce ecomic efficiency. Efforts to increase demand for American workers through restricting imports or to increase demand for skilled workers by 497restricting the supply of labor reduce efficiency as well. In each case& the wage gain will increase the cost of producing the good or service and thus shift its supply curve to the left. Such efforts& if successful& increase the earnings of union members by creating higher prices and smaller quantities for consumers. They may also reduce the profitability of their employers.
Other attempts by unions to raise wages by increasing the demand for their members are t likely to create inefficiency. For example& union efforts to increase worker productivity or to encourage consumers to buy products made by union members do t reduce ecomic efficiency.
In the case of bilateral mopoly& the amount of labor employed is restricted by the mopsony firm to a quantity that falls short of the efficient level. In effect& the efficiency damage has already been done. The labor union seeks merely to offset the mopsony firm’s ability to restrict the wage.
Are unions successful in their primary goal of increasing wages? An examina of the impact on wages by firms that faced organizing drives by unions between 1984 and 1999 found virtually change in wages attributable to union organizing efforts. The study examined firms in which unions had either barely won or had barely lost the elec. It found that unions that had eked out victories had gone on to organize workers& but had had significant impact on wages or on productivity (Dinardo& J.& and David S. Lee& 2004). Other evidence& however& suggests that unions do tend to raise wages for their members. Controlling for other factors that affect wages& over the period 1973 to 2002& unions appear to have increased wages by about 17% on average (Blanchflower& D. G.& and Alex Bryson& 2004). Part of the explana of this finding is that unions have had the most success in organizing in the public sector& where union pressure for higher wages is most likely to be successful.
Other Suppliers and Mopoly Power
Just as workers can unionize to gain a degree of mopoly power in the marketplace& so other suppliers can organize with a similar goal. Two of the most important types of organizas aimed at garnering market power are professional associas and producers’ cooperatives.
Professional Associas
Professional people generally belong to organizas that represent their interests. For example& physicians in the United States belong to the American Medical Associa (AMA)& and lawyers belong to the American Bar Associa (ABA). Both organizas work vigorously to advance the ecomic interests of their members.
Professional organizas often lobby for legisla that protects their members. They may seek to limit competi by limiting the number of individuals who can be licensed to practice a particular profession. The AMA has been very successful in limiting the number of physicians& thus maintaining higher salaries than would otherwise exist. The ABA has fought legal reforms aimed at limiting awards to plaintiffs who win damage suits; such reforms would be likely to reduce the incomes of lawyers.
Producers’ Cooperatives 498
Independent producers sometimes band together into a cooperative for the purpose of selling their products. The cooperative sets the price and assigns produc quotas to individual firms. In effect& a cooperative acts as a cartel.
Because they violate the provisions of laws that outlaw such arrangements in most industries& producers’ cooperatives must be authorized by Congress. Farmers have sometimes been given such rights when they are confronted by mopsony buyers. For example& Congress granted dairy farmers the right to form cooperatives in the 1920s because they faced mopsony buyers. High transporta costs for fresh milk& together with ecomies of scale in processing milk& generally left only one dairy processor to buy raw milk from dairy farmers in a particular area. By forming a cooperative& farmers could counter the mopsony power of a processor with the mopoly power of their own& creating a bilateral mopoly.
Today& with much lower transporta costs& dairy farmers can deal with a naal market so that processors longer have mopsony power. But dairy farmers continue to have the right to form cooperatives. As we have seen in an earlier chapter& dairy farmers also enjoy protec from federal programs that are designed to keep dairy prices high.
Key Takeaways
A firm that has mopoly power in the supply of a factor makes choices in the same manner as any other mopoly firm; it maximizes profit by selecting a level of output at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost and selling that output at a price determined by the demand curve.
Unions have tradially sought to raise wages and to improve working condis by exerting market power over the supply of labor.
In bilateral mopoly& a mopsony buyer faces a mopoly seller. Prices in the model are indeterminate.
Professional associas often seek market power through their influence on government policy.
Producers’ cooperatives& a form of legal cartel& have been organized in some agricultural markets in an effort to offset the perceived mopsony power of some buyers of agricultural products.

Case in Point: Unions and the Airline Industry
figureure 14.13 Daniel Mennerich – London Heathrow U.K. – CC BY-NC-ND 2.0.
499
Unions represent 60% of the nmanagerial employees of U.S. airlines. And labor costs make up one-third of airline costs. All employees have a stake in the success of the firms for which they work. That is certainly the case for the major unions representing airline employees. Both union leaders and airline management have much to gain from a relaship that benefits both employees and the airlines that employ them.
That sort of relaship has t always existed. In 1981& for example& Continental Airlines hired Frank Lorenzo& an airline entrepreneur& to run Continental. The airline had lost money the previous three years. Mr. Lorenzo promptly abrogated Continental’s contracts with employees& and told them that they could go back to work but only at sharply reduced wages. Continental’s pilots& flight attendants& and ground crews declared strikes against the airline. The airline was able to break the strike by hiring replacement employees. Even so& Continental declared bankruptcy in 1983. Mr. Lorenzo told striking employees that they could return to work& but they could do so only by agreeing to work at half their previous wage. Continental’s strategy of union suppression achieved reducs in wage costs& but those savings had a cost as well. A demoralized labor force produced dramatic reducs in the quality of service& and Continental was back in bankruptcy in 1991. In 1986& 6&000 members of the Internaal Federa of Flight Attendants (IFFA) declared a strike against TWA. The airline followed a strategy similar to Continental’s and was able to break the strike by hiring replacement employees. After 10 weeks& the IFFA declared an uncondial end to the strike and sought to have its members rehired. It was t until three and a half years later that all 6&000 got their jobs back. Ultimately& TWA went out of business.
t all airlines have had the same unhappy relaships with unions. Southwest Airlines& which started as a nunion airline& w operates with a largely unionized labor force. It has continued its strategy of paying high wages and including employees in management decisions. The result has been one of the highest profit margins in the industry together with high productivity of both workers and aircraft.
Continental has also emerged as a “different” airline. More recently& it hired a new Chief Executive Officer who quickly returned the airline to profitability and established a new workplace culture in which employees were given a role in managerial decisions and were hired based in part on their teamwork skills. Continental has been able to shed its old500reputa as a union suppressor and has established itself as an airline that works well with unions and has a minimum degree of conflict.
Ather approach to dealing with airline employees has been to include them in ownership. United employees& for example& own the airline. Other airlines in which employees have had a substantial ownership role include Western Airlines& Eastern Airlines& rthwest& Delta Airlines& and United. In each case& employees exchanged equity for wage concessions. Each of these airlines implemented an Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP). In each case& the program began with great optimism on the part of management and labor& but in most cases& conflicts between workers and employers quickly emerged. Western and Eastern abandoned their ESOP programs after two years. While nearly all the ESOP arrangements initially increased profits& ne of them was accompanied by any structural change in the labor-management relaship. Ultimately& all of these plans generated disappointing results. Clearly& the mere crea of a system in which employees own a share of the airline is t sufficient; changes in the structure of the labor-management relas must occur as well. Some airlines have managed to prosper in a difficult ecomic world. The key to success seems to lie in the establishment of workplace culture that rewards good teamwork and efforts to enhance productivity. Airlines such as Southwest and the “new” Continental demonstrate that an airline can work effectively with unions& pay high wages& and still be profitable. Sources: Jody Hoffer Gittell& Andrew von rdenflycht& and Thomas A. Kochan& “Mutual Gains or Zero Sum? Labor Relas and Firm Performance in the Airline Industry&” Industrial and Labor Relas Review& 57: 2 (January 2004): 163–80; and Sandra L. Albrecht& “‘We are on Strike!’ The Development of Labor Militancy in the Airline Industry&” Labor History& 45:1 (February 2004): 101–17.
Answer to Try It! Problem
Any wage negotiated between the mopsony (the firm hiring the labor) and the mopoly (the union representing the labor) that falls between Wm and Wu will lead to a quantity of labor employed that is greater than Lm. The por of the supply curve below the negotiated wage becomes irrelevant since the firm cant hire workers for those wages. The supply curve thus becomes a horizontal line at the negotiated wage until the negotiated wage intersects the supply curve; at wages higher than the negotiated wage& the existing supply curve is operative. Up to the quantity of labor at the intersec of the negotiated wage and the supply curve& the wage and MFC are the same. At any wage between Wm and Wu& the firm will maximize profit by employing labor where MRP and MFC are equal& and this will occur at a quantity of labor that is greater than Lm.

Summary
Factor markets diverge from perfect competi whenever buyers and/or sellers are price setters rather than price takers. A firm that is the sole purchaser of a factor is a mopsony. The distinguishing feature of the applica of the marginal decision rule to mopsony is that the MFC of the factor exceeds its price. Less of the factor is used than would be the case if the factor were demanded by many firms. The price paid by the mopsony firm is determined from the factor supply curve; it is less than the competitive price would be. The lower quantity and lower price that occur in a mopsony factor market arise from features of the market that are directly analogous to the higher product price and lower produc quantity chosen in mopoly markets. A price floor (e.g.& a minimum wage) can induce a mopsony to increase its use of a factor.
Sellers can also exercise power to set price. A factor can be sold by a mopoly firm& which is likely to behave in a way that corresponds to the mopoly model.
When there are a large number of sellers& they may band together in an organiza that seeks to exert a degree of mopoly power on their behalf. Workers (sellers of labor)& for example& have organized unions to seek better wages and working condis. This goal can be accomplished by restricting the available supply or by increasing the demand for labor. When a union represents all of a mopsony firm’s workers& a bilateral mopoly exists. A bilateral mopoly results in a kind of price-setters’ standoff& in which the firm seeks a low wage and the union a high one.
Professional associas may seek to improve the ecomic posi of their members by supporting legisla that reduces supply or raises demand. Some agricultural producers join producers’ cooperatives to exert some power over price and output. Agricultural cooperatives must be authorized by Congress; otherwise& they would violate laws against collusion in the marketplace.

Start Up: Trade Winds
Rapid increases in the flow of goods and services between vastly different nas and cultures have changed how people eat& how they dress& and even how they communicate with one ather. For you& increased trade has meant greater choice of what to buy and often lower prices.
Look through your room. Chances are it is full of items from all around the world. The relatively free trade that exists today provides you with expanded choices. one forced you to buy that shirt from India or that CD player from Japan. Presumably you bought them because you preferred them to other shirts and CD players you could have bought& perhaps because they had certain characteristics—style& color& perceived quality& or price—that you favored.
Your gains are being experienced worldwide because the winds of internaal trade have blown generally freer in the past decades. Nas all over the world have dramatically lowered the barriers they impose on the products of other countries.
One region that was once closed to virtually all trade but is w open is Eastern Europe and the countries that made up the former Soviet Union. A key part of these countries’ attempts to create market capitalist ecomic systems has been the opening of their borders to internaal trade.
In Western Europe& the members of the European Union (EU) have eliminated virtually every restric on the free flow of goods and services among them. A truckload of electronic equipment from Italy w passes through France on its way to Spain with more restrics than would be encountered by a truck delivering goods from Michigan to Illiis. The purchase of the equipment can even be arranged using a new currency& the euro& which has been adopted by most EU nas.
Canada& Mexico& and the United States& while t adopting a common currency& have created a similar free trade area& the rth American Free Trade Area (NAFTA). In addi& the 18 member nas of the Asia Pacific Ecomic Coopera organiza (APEC) agreed in 1994 to forge a free trade area among industrialized nas such as the United States and Japan by 2010. Other member nas such as Mexico and China agreed to participate by 2020.
NAFTA has resulted in a dramatic increase in trade between Canada& the United States& and Mexico. Since NAFTA’s crea in 1994& employment in all three countries has risen substantially. Those increases in employment cant necessarily be attributed to NAFTA& but the fact that they have occurred flies in the face of the arguments when NAFTA was first proposed that it would lead to a reduc in U.S. employment.
President Bush proposed and Congress passed in 2005 the crea of a Central American Free Trade Associa (CAFTA) that would create a free trade area south of Mexico and linked to the United States. It abolishes tariffs on goods traded between the United States and Costa Rica& the Dominican 568
Republic& El Salvador& Guatemala& Honduras& and Nicaragua. The six countries make up the secd-largest export market for the United States in Latin America& behind Mexico. President Bush has also proposed extending a free trade zone throughout the Western Hemisphere.
And& in 1995& the World Trade Organiza (WTO) was established to “help trade flow smoothly& freely& fairly and predictably” among member nas. In 2008& it had 153 member countries. Since World War II& the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)—WTO’s predecessor—and WTO have generated a series of agreements that slashed trade restraints among members. These agreements have helped propel internaal trade& which in 2006 was more than 35 times its level in 1950& but the negotias leading to these agreements have always been protracted and tumultuous and issues of naalism and patriotism are often t far from the surface. The eighth and ninth round of trade talks are referred to as the Doha Round& because they were officially launched in Doha& Qatar& in 2001. In mid-2008& talks were still mired in controversy over the removal of agricultural export subsidies and lowering of trade barriers of various kinds.
Why have so many countries moved to make trade freer? What are the effects of free trade? Why do efforts to eliminate trade restrics meet with resistance? Why do many nas continue to impose barriers against foreign goods and services? How do such barriers affect the ecomy? How do such barriers affect you?
This chapter will answer these quess by developing a model of internaal trade based on the concept of comparative advantage& introduced in an earlier chapter. The model predicts that free internaal trade will benefit the countries that participate in it. Free trade does t benefit every individual& however. Most people benefit from free trade& but some are hurt. We will then look at the phemen of two-way trade& in which countries both import and export the same goods. The last part of the chapter examines the effects of trade restrics and evaluates the arguments made for such restrics. Ecomists tend to be skeptical of their validity.

Learning Objectives

To model the effects of trade& we begin by looking at a hypothetical country that does t engage in trade and see how its produc and consump change when it does engage in trade.
Produc and Consump Without Internaal Trade
Suppose the hypothetical country of Roadway is completely isolated from the rest of the world. It neither exports r imports goods and services. We shall use the produc possibilities model to analyze Roadway’s ability to produce goods and services.
A produc possibilities curve illustrates the produc choices available to an ecomy. Recall that the produc possibilities curve for a particular country is determined by the factors of produc and techlogy available to it. 570
figureure 17.1 “Roadway’s Produc Possibilities Curve” shows a produc possibilities curve for Roadway. We assume that it produces only two goods—trucks and boats. Roadway must be operating somewhere on its produc possibilities curve or it will be wasting resources or engaging in inefficient produc. If it is operating inside the curve at a point such as D& then a combina on the curve& such as B& would provide more of both goods (Roadway produces 3&000 more trucks and 3&000 more boats per year at B than at D). At any point inside the curve& Roadway’s produc would t be efficient. Point E suggests an even higher level of output than points A& B& or C& but because point E lies outside Roadway’s produc possibilities curve& it cant be attained.
figureure 17.1 Roadway’s Produc Possibilities Curve
The produc possibilities curve for Roadway shows the combinas of trucks and boats that it can produce& given the factors of produc and techlogy available to it. To maximize the value of total produc& Roadway must be operating somewhere along this curve. Produc at point D implies that Roadway is failing to use its resources fully and efficiently; produc at point E is ubtainable.
We have learned that the absolute value of the slope of a produc possibilities curve at any point gives the quantity of the good on the vertical axis that must be given up to produce an addial unit of the good on the horizontal axis. It thus gives the opportunity cost of producing ather unit of the good on the horizontal axis. 571
figureure 17.2 Measuring Opportunity Cost in Roadway
The slope of the produc possibilities curve at any point is equal to the slope of a line tangent to the curve at that point. The absolute value of the slope equals the opportunity cost of increased boat produc. Moving down and to the right along its produc possibilities curve& the opportunity cost of boat produc increases; this is an applica of the law of increasing opportunity cost.
figureure 17.2 “Measuring Opportunity Cost in Roadway” shows the opportunity cost of producing boats at points A& B& and C. Recall that the slope of a curve at any point is equal to the slope of a line drawn tangent to the curve at that point. The slope of a line tangent to the produc possibilities curve at point B& for example& is −1. The opportunity cost of producing one more boat is thus one truck. As the law of increasing opportunity costs predicts& in order to produce more boats& Roadway must give up more and more trucks for each addial boat. Roadway’s opportunity cost of producing boats increases as we travel down and to the right on its produc possibilities curve.
Comparative Advantage
People participate in internaal trade because they make themselves better off by doing so. In this sec we will find that countries that participate in internaal trade are able to consume more of all goods and services than they could consume while producing in isola from the rest of the world. 572
Suppose the world consists of two countries& Roadway and Seaside. Their produc possibilities curves are given in figureure 17.3 “Comparative Advantage in Roadway and Seaside”. 575 Specializa and the Gains from Trade
We have so far assumed that trade occurs between Roadway and Seaside. w let us assume that trade opens up. The fact that the opportunity costs differ between the two countries suggests the possibility for mutually advantageous trade. The opportunities created by trade will induce a greater degree of specializa in both countries& specializa that reflects comparative advantage.
Trade and Specializa
Before trade& truck producers in Roadway could exchange a truck for half a boat. In Seaside& however& a truck could be exchanged for five boats. Once trade opens between the two countries& truck producers in Roadway will rush to export trucks to Seaside.
Boat producers in Seaside enjoy a similar bonanza. Before trade& one of their boats could be exchanged for one-fifth of a truck. By shipping their boats to Roadway& they can get two trucks for each boat. Boat producers in Seaside will rush to export boats to Roadway.
Once trade between Roadway and Seaside begins& the terms of trade& the rate at which a country can trade domestic products for imported products& will seek market equilibrium. The final terms of trade will lie somewhere between one-half boats for one truck found in Roadway and five boats for one truck in Seaside. Suppose the terms of trade are one boat for one truck. (How the specific terms of trade are actually determined is t important for this discussion. It is eugh to kw that the final terms of trade will lie somewhere between Seaside’s and Roadway’s opportunity costs for boat and truck produc.) Roadway’s truck producers will w get one boat per truck—a far better exchange than was available to them before trade.
Roadway’s manufacturers will move to produce more trucks and fewer boats until they reach the point on their produc possibilities curve at which the terms of trade equals the opportunity cost of producing trucks. This occurs at point B in Panel (a) of figureure 17.5 “Internaal Trade Induces Greater Specializa”; Roadway w produces 7&000 trucks and 7&000 boats per year. 576
figureure 17.5 Internaal Trade Induces Greater Specializa
Before trade& Roadway is producing at point A in Panel (a) and Seaside is producing at point A′ in Panel (b). The terms of trade are one& meaning that one boat exchanges for one truck. Roadside moves along its produc possibilities curve to point B& at which the curve has a slope of −1. Roadside will produce more trucks (and fewer boats). Seaside moves along its produc possibilities curve to point B′& at which the slope equals −1. Seaside will produce more boats (and fewer trucks). Trade leads each country in the direc of producing more of the good in which it has a comparative advantage.
Similarly& Seaside will specialize more in boat produc. As shown in Panel (b) of figureure 17.5 “Internaal Trade Induces Greater Specializa”& producers will shift resources out of truck produc and into boat produc until they reach the point on their produc possibilities curve at which the terms of trade equals the opportunity cost of producing boats. This occurs at point B′; Seaside produces 3&000 trucks and 6&000 boats per year.
We see that trade between the two countries causes each country to specialize in the good in which it has a comparative advantage. Roadway produces more trucks& and Seaside produces more boats. The specializa is t& however& complete. The law of increasing opportunity cost means that& as an ecomy moves along its produc possibilities curve& the cost of addial units rises. An ecomy with a comparative advantage in a particular good will expand its produc of that good only up to the point where its opportunity cost equals the terms of trade.
As a result of trade& Roadway w produces more trucks and fewer boats. Seaside produces more boats and fewer trucks. Through exchange& however& both countries are likely to end up consuming more of both goods.
figureure 17.6 “The Mutual Benefits of Trade” shows one such possibility. Suppose Roadway ships 2&500 trucks per year to Seaside in exchange for 2&500 boats& as shown in the table in figureure 17.6 “The Mutual Benefits of Trade”. Roadway thus emerges with 4&500 trucks (the 7&000 it produces at B minus the 2&500 it ships) and 9&500 boats. It has 500 more of each good than it did before trade. The precise amounts of each good shipped will depend on demand and supply. The essential point is that Roadway will produce more of the good—trucks—in which it has a comparative advantage. It will export that good to a country& or countries& that has a comparative advantage in something else. 577
figureure 17.6 The Mutual Benefits of Trade
Roadway and Seaside each consume more of both goods when there is trade between them. The table shows values of produc before trade (BT) and after trade (AT). As shown in Panel (a) and in the exhibit’s table& Roadway exports 2&500 trucks to Seaside in exchange for 2&500 boats and ends up consuming at point C& which is outside its produc possibilities curve. Similarly& in Panel (b)& Seaside ends up consuming at point C′& which is outside its produc possibilities curve. Trade allows both countries to consume more than they are capable of producing.
How does Seaside fare? When trade began& factors of produc shifted into boat produc& in which Seaside had a comparative advantage. Seaside tripled its produc of boats—from 2&000 per year to 6&000 per year. It sends 2&500 of those boats to Roadway& so it ends up with 3&500 boats per year. It reduces its produc of trucks to 3&000 per year& but receives 2&500 more from Roadway. That leaves it with 5&500. Seaside emerges from the opening of trade with 1&500 more boats and 750 more trucks than it had before trade.
As Roadway trades trucks for boats& its produc remains at point B. But it w consumes combina C; it has more of both goods than it had at A& the solu before trade. Seaside’s produc remains at point B′& but it w consumes at point C′& where it has more trucks and more boats than it had before trade.
Although all countries can increase their consump through trade& t everyone in those countries will be happy with the result. In the case of Roadway and Seaside& for example& some boat producers in Roadway will be displaced as cheaper boats arrive from Seaside. Some truck producers in Seaside will be displaced as cheaper trucks arrive from Roadway. The produc possibilities model suggests that the resources displaced will ultimately find more productive uses. They will produce trucks in Roadway and boats in Seaside. But there will be a period of painful transi as workers and owners of capital and natural resources move from one activity to ather. That transi will be completed when the two countries are back on their respective produc possibilities curves. Full employment will be restored& which means both countries will be back at the same level of employment they had before trade.
The table in figureure 17.6 “The Mutual Benefits of Trade” shows the produc and consump possibilities for the two countries before and after trade. The graphs in the figureure show the produc and consump points on the produc possibilities curves of both countries. tice that each country produces on its produc possibilities curve& but internaal trade allows both countries to consume a combina of goods they would be incapable of producing! 578
We see this same phemen in individual households. Each household specializes in an activity in which it has a comparative advantage. For one household& that may be landscaping& for ather& it may be the practice of medicine& for ather it may be the provision of childcare. Whatever the activity& specializa allows each household to earn income that can be used to purchase housing& food& clothing& and so on. Imagine for a moment how your household would fare if it had to produce every good or service it consumed. The members of a household would work very hard& but it is inconceivable that the household could survive if it relied on itself for everything it consumed. By specializing in the activity in which each individual has a comparative advantage& people are able to consume far more than they could produce themselves.
Despite the transial problems affecting some factors of produc& the potential benefits from free trade are large. For this reason& most ecomists are strongly in favor of opening markets and extending internaal trade throughout the world. The ecomic case has been a powerful force in moving the world toward freer trade.
Key Takeaways
In order to maximize the value of its output& a country must be producing a combina of goods and services that lies on its produc possibilities curve.
Suppose two countries each produce two goods and their opportunity costs differ. If this is the case& there is an opportunity for trade between the two countries that will leave both better off.
Internaal trade leads countries to specialize in goods and services in which they have a comparative advantage.
The terms of trade determine the extent to which each country will specialize. Each will increase produc of the good or service in which it has a comparative advantage up to the point where the opportunity cost of producing it equals the terms of trade.
Free internaal trade can increase the availability of all goods and services in all the countries that participate in it. Trade allows countries to consume combinas of goods and services they would be unable to produce.
While free trade increases the total quantity of goods and services available to each country& there are both winners and losers in the short run.

582 17.2 Two-Way Trade
Learning Objectives
Distinguish between one-way trade and two-way trade.
Explain why two-way trade may occur.
The model of trade presented thus far assumed that countries specialize in producing the good in which they have a comparative advantage and& therefore& engage in one-way trade. One-way (or interindustry) trade occurs when countries specialize in producing the goods in which they have a comparative advantage and then export those goods so they can import the goods in which they do t have a comparative advantage.
However& when we look at world trade& we also see countries exchanging the same goods or goods in the same industry category. For example& the United States may both export construc materials to Canada and import them from Canada. American car buyers can choose Chevrolets& Fords& and Chryslers. They can also purchase imported cars such as Toyotas. Japanese car buyers may choose to purchase Toyotas—or imported cars such as Chevrolets& Fords& and Chryslers. The United States imports cars from Japan and exports cars to it. Conversely& Japan imports cars from the United States and exports cars to it. Internaal trade in which countries both import and export the same or similar goods is called two-way (or intraindustry) trade.
Two reasons countries import and export the same goods are varias in transporta costs and seasonal effects. In the example of the United States and Canada both importing and exporting construc materials& transporta costs are the likely explana. It may be cheaper for a contractor in rthern Maine to import construc materials from the eastern part of Canada than to buy them in the United States. For a contractor in Vancouver& British Columbia& it may be cheaper to import construc materials from somewhere in the western part of the United States than to buy them in Canada. By engaging in trade& both the American and Canadian contractors save on transporta costs. Seasonal factors explain why the United States both imports fruit from Chile and exports fruit to Chile.
Ather explana of two-way trade in similar goods lies in recognizing that t all goods are produced under condis of perfect competi. Once this assump is relaxed& we can explain two-way trade in terms of a feature of mopolistic competi and some cases of oligopoly: product differentia. Suppose two countries have similar endowments of factors of produc and techlogies available to them& but their products are differentiated—clocks produced by different manufacturers& for example& are different. Consumers in the United States buy some clocks produced in Switzerland& just as consumers in Switzerland purchase some clocks produced in the United States. Indeed& if two countries are similar in their relative endowments of factors of produc and in the techlogies available to them& two-way trade based on product differentia is likely to be more significant than one-way trade based on comparative advantage. 583
Two-way trade based on product differentia may entail lower adjustment costs. In the case of two-way trade& there is specializa within industries rather than movement of factors of produc out of industries that compete with newly imported goods and into export industries. Such adjustments are likely to be faster and less painful for labor and for the owners of the capital and natural resources involved.
Because two-way trade often occurs in the context of imperfect competi& we cant expect it to meet the efficiency standards of one-way trade based on comparative advantage and the underlying assump of perfectly competitive markets. But& as we discussed in the chapter on imperfect competi& the inefficiency must be weighed against the benefits derived from product differentia. People in the United States are t limited to buying only the kinds of cars produced in the United States& just as people in Japan are t limited to buying only the cars produced in Japan.
Key Takeaways
Specializa and trade according to comparative advantage leads to one-way trade.
A large percentage of trade among countries with similar factor endowments is two-way trade& in which countries import and export the same or similar goods and services.
Two-way trade is often explained by varias in transporta costs and seasonal factors; in similar goods& it often occurs in the context of models of imperfect competi.
Adjustment costs associated with expansion of two-way trade may be lower than for expansion of one-way trade.
