586 17.3 Restrics on Internaal Trade
Learning Objectives
Define the term protecist policy and illustrate the general impact in a market subject to a protecist policy.
Describe the various forms of protecist policy.
Discuss and assess the arguments used to justify trade restrics.
In spite of the strong theoretical case that can be made for free internaal trade& every country in the world has erected at least some barriers to trade. Trade restrics are typically undertaken in an effort to protect companies and workers in the home ecomy from competi by foreign firms. A protecist policy is one in which a country restricts the importa of goods and services produced in foreign countries. The slowdown in the ecomy late in 2007 and in 2008 has produced a new round of protecist sentiment—one that became explicit in the 2008 U.S. presidential campaign.
The United States& for example& uses protecist policies to limit the quantity of foreign-produced sugar that can enter the United States. The effect of this policy is to reduce the supply of sugar in the U.S. market and increase the price of sugar in the United States. The 2008 U.S. Farm Bill sweetened things for sugar growers even more: it raised the price they are guaranteed to receive and limited imports of foreign sugar so that American growers will always have at least 85% of the domestic market. The bill for the first time set an income limit—only growers whose incomes fall below $1.5 million per year (for couples) or $750&000 for individuals will receive federal subsidies (The Wall Street Journal& 2008).
The U.S. price of sugar is almost triple the world price of sugar& thus reducing the quantity consumed in the United States. The program benefits growers of sugar beets and sugar cane at the expense of consumers. 587
figureure 17.10 The Impact of Protecist Policies
Protecist policies reduce the quantities of foreign goods and services supplied to the country that imposes the restric. As a result& such policies shift the supply curve to the left for the good or service whose imports are restricted. In the case shown& the supply curve shifts to S2& the equilibrium price rises to P2& and the equilibrium quantity falls to Q2.
Source: Historical Statistics& Colonial Times to 1970: Statistical Abstract of the United States 1998& Table . 1325; Statistical Abstract of the United States& 1990; U.S. Internaal Commission (http://dataweb.usitc.gov/prepared_reports.asp).
In general& protecist policies imposed for a particular good always reduce its supply& raise its price& and reduce the equilibrium quantity& as shown in figureure 17.11 “U.S. Tariff Rates& 1820–2005”. Protec often takes the form of an import tax or a limit on the amount that can be imported& but it can also come in the form of voluntary export restrics and other barriers.
Tariffs
A tariff is a tax on imported goods and services. The average tariff on dutiable imports in the United States (that is& those imports on which a tariff is imposed) is about 4%. Some imports have much higher tariffs. For example& the U.S. tariff on imported frozen orange juice is 35 cents per gallon (which amounts to about 40% of value). The tariff on imported canned tuna is 35%& and the tariff on imported shoes ranges between 2% and 48%.
A tariff raises the cost of selling imported goods. It thus shifts the supply curve for goods to the left& as in figureure 17.10 “The Impact of Protecist Policies”. A tariff raises the price of the good and reduces the quantity sold. The revenue from the tariff goes to the government. The burden of the tariff is shared by consumers& whose consumer surplus falls& and producers of the imported goods& whose producer surplus falls. The gain to domestic producers of the good and to the government in tariff revenue is less than the total loss& and so the net welfare to consumers falls. 588
Antidumping Proceedings
One of the most common protecist measures w in use is the antidumping proceeding. A domestic firm& faced with competi by a foreign competitor& files charges with its government that the foreign firm is dumping& or charging an “unfair” price. Under rules spelled out in internaal negotias that preceded approval of the World Trade Organiza& an unfair price was defined as a price below produc cost or below the price the foreign firm charges for the same good in its own country. While these definis may seem straightforward eugh& they have proven to be quite troublesome. The defini of “produc cost” is a thoroughly arbitrary procedure. In defining cost& the government agency invariably includes a specifica of “rmal” profit. That rmal profit can be absurdly high. The United States Department of Justice& which is the U.S. agency in charge of determining whether a foreign firm has charged an unfair price& has sometimes defined rmal profit rates as exceeding produc cost by well over 50%& a rate far higher than exists in most of industry.
The practice of a foreign firm charging a price in the United States that is below the price it charges in its own country is common. The U.S. market may be more competitive& or the foreign firm may simply be trying to make its product attractive to U.S. buyers that are t yet accustomed to its product. In any event& such price discrimina behavior is t unusual and is t necessarily “unfair.”
In the United States& once the Department of Justice has determined that a foreign firm is guilty of charging an unfair price& the U.S. Internaal Trade Commission must determine that the foreign firm has done material harm to the U.S. firm. If a U.S. firm has suffered a reduc in sales and thus in employment it will typically be found to have suffered material harm& and punitive duties will be imposed.
Quotas
A quota is a direct restric on the total quantity of a good or service that may be imported during a specific period. Quotas restrict total supply and therefore increase the domestic price of the good or service on which they are imposed. Quotas generally specify that an exporting country’s share of a domestic market may t exceed a certain limit.
In some cases& quotas are set to raise the domestic price to a particular level. Congress requires the Department of Agriculture& for example& to impose quotas on imported sugar to keep the wholesale price in the United States above 22 cents per pound. The world price is typically less than 10 cents per pound.
A quota restricting the quantity of a particular good imported into an ecomy shifts the supply curve to the left& as in figureure 17.10 “The Impact of Protecist Policies”. It raises price and reduces quantity.
An important distinc between quotas and tariffs is that quotas do t increase costs to foreign producers. Indeed& a quota raises price but t costs of produc and thus may increase profits. Because the quota imposes a limit on quantity& any profits it creates in other countries will t induce the entry of new firms that ordinarily eliminate profits in perfect competi. By defini& entry of new foreign firms to earn the profits available in the United States is blocked by the quota.
589 Voluntary Export Restrics
Voluntary export restrics are a form of trade barrier by which foreign firms agree to limit the quantity of goods exported to a particular country. They became prominent in the United States in the 1980s& when the U.S. government persuaded foreign exporters of automobiles and steel to agree to limit their exports to the United States.
Although such restrics are called voluntary& they typically are agreed to only after pressure is applied by the country whose industries they protect. The United States& for example& has succeeded in pressuring many countries to accept quotas limiting their exports of goods ranging from sweaters to steel.
A voluntary export restric works precisely like an ordinary quota. It raises prices for the domestic product and reduces the quantity consumed of the good or service affected by the quota. It can also increase the profits of firms that agree to the quota because it raises the price they receive for their products.
Other Barriers
In addi to tariffs and quotas& measures such as safety standards& labeling requirements& pollu controls& and quality restrics all may have the effect of restricting imports.
Many restrics aimed at protecting consumers in the domestic market create barriers as a purely unintended& and probably desirable& side effect. For example& limitas on insecticide levels in foods are often more strict in the United States than in other countries. These standards tend to discourage the import of foreign goods& but their primary purpose appears to be to protect consumers from harmful chemicals& t to restrict trade. But some ntariff barriers seem to serve purpose other than to keep foreign goods out. Tomatoes produced in Mexico& for example& compete with those produced in the United States. But Mexican tomatoes tend to be smaller than U.S. tomatoes. The United States once imposed size restrics to “protect” U.S. consumers from small tomatoes. The result was a highly effective trade barrier that protected U.S. producers and raised U.S. tomato prices. These restrics were abolished under terms of the rth American Free Trade Agreement& which has led to a large increase in U.S. imports of Mexican tomatoes and a reduc in U.S. tomato produc (Guajardo& R. G.& and Homero A. Elizondo& 2003).
590 Justificas for Trade Restric: An Evalua
The conceptual justifica for free trade is one of the oldest arguments in ecomics; there is disputing the logic of the argument that free trade increases global produc& worldwide consump& and internaal efficiency. But critics stress that the argument is a theoretical one. In the real world& they say& there are several arguments that can be made to justify protecist measures.
Infant Industries
One argument for trade barriers is that they serve as a kind of buffer to protect fledgling domestic industries. Initially& firms in a new industry may be too small to achieve significant ecomies of scale and could be clobbered by established firms in other countries. A new domestic industry with potential ecomies of scale is called an infant industry.
Consider the situa in which firms in a country are attempting to enter a new industry in which many large firms already exist in the internaal arena. The foreign firms have taken advantage of ecomies of scale and have therefore achieved relatively low levels of produc costs. New firms& facing low levels of output and higher average costs& may find it difficult to compete. The infant industry argument suggests that by offering protec during an industry’s formative years& a tariff or quota may allow the new industry to develop and prosper.

591
figureure 17.11 “U.S. Tariff Rates& 1820–2005” shows average tariff rates on dutiable imports in the United States since 1820. The high tariffs of the early nineteenth century were typically justified as being necessary to allow U.S. firms to gain a competitive foothold in the world ecomy. As domestic industries became established& rates fell. Subsequent increases in tariffs were a response in part to internal crises: the Civil War and the Great Depression. Tariff rates have fallen dramatically since 1930.
Critics of the infant industry argument say that once protec is in place& it may be very difficult to remove. Inefficient firms& they contend& may be able to survive for long periods under the umbrella of infant industry protec.
Strategic Trade Policy
A new version of the infant industry argument has been used in the past few years as techlogical developments have spawned whole new industries and transformed existing ones. The new version of the infant industry argument assumes an imperfectly competitive market.
Suppose techlogical change has given rise to a new industry. Given the ecomies of scale in this industry& a few firms are likely to dominate it worldwide—it will likely emerge as an oligopoly. The firms that dominate the industry are likely to earn ecomic profits that will persist. Furthermore& because there will be only a few firms& they will be located in only a few countries. Their governments could conceivably impose taxes on these firms’ profits that would enhance ecomic well-being within the country. The potential for such gains may justify government efforts to assist firms seeking to acquire a dominant posi in the new industry.
Government aid could take the form of protecist trade policies aimed at allowing these firms to expand in the face of foreign competi& assistance with research and development efforts& programs to provide workers with special skills needed by the industry& or subsidies in the form of direct payments or special tax treatment. Any policy aimed at promoting the development of key industries that may increase a country’s domestic well-being through trade with the rest of the world is kwn as a strategic trade policy.
Although strategic trade policy suggests a conceptually positive role for government in internaal trade& proponents of the approach te that it has dangers. Firms might use the strategic trade argument even if their development were unlikely to offer the gains specified in the theory. The successful applica of the approach requires that the government correctly identify industries in which a country can& in fact& achieve dominance—something that may t be possible. Various European governments provided subsidies to firms that were involved in the produc of Airbus& which is w a major competitor in the airplane industry. On the other hand& Britain and France subsidized the development of the supersonic plane called the Concorde. After a few Concordes had been produced& it became obvious that the aircraft was a financially losing proposi and produc was halted. The airline has w gone out of business.
Finally& those firms whose success strategic trade policy promotes might have sufficient political clout to block the taxes that would redistribute the gains of the policies to the popula in general. Thus& the promise of strategic trade policy is unlikely to be fulfilled.
592 Naal security
It is sometimes argued that the security of the United States would be threatened if this country depended on foreign powers as the primary source of strategic materials. In time of war& the United States might be cut off from sources of foreign supply and lose some of the materials upon which U.S. industry depends.
One area where the naal security argument is applied is the oil industry. Given the volatility of the political situa in the Middle East& some people say& the United States should protect the domestic oil industry in order to ensure adequate produc capability in the event Middle Eastern supplies are cut off.
An alternative to tariff protec of strategic commodities is to stockpile those commodities for use in a crisis. For example& the United States maintains a strategic petroleum reserve for use in case of a cutoff in foreign supplies or domestic crises. For example& strategic oil reserves were tapped in the wake of pipeline and refinery disrups following Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
Job Protec
The desire to maintain existing jobs threatened by foreign competi is probably the single most important source of today’s protecist policies. Some industries that at one time had a comparative advantage are longer among the world’s lowest-cost producers; they struggle to stay afloat. Cost cutting leads to layoffs& and layoffs lead to demands for protec.
The model of internaal trade in perfect competi suggests that trade will threaten some industries. As countries specialize in activities in which they have a comparative advantage& sectors in which they do t have this advantage will shrink. Maintaining those sectors through trade barriers blocks a na from enjoying the gains possible from free trade.
A further difficulty with the use of trade barriers to shore up employment in a particular sector is that it may be an ermously expensive strategy. Suppose eugh of a foreign good is kept out of the United States to save one U.S. job. That shifts the supply curve slightly to the left& raising prices for U.S. consumers and reducing consumer surplus. The loss to consumers is the cost per job saved. Estimates of the cost of saving one job in the steel industry through restrics on steel imports& for example& go as high as $800&000 per year.
Cheap Foreign Labor and Outsourcing
One reason often given for the perceived need to protect American workers against free internaal trade is that workers must be protected against cheap foreign labor. This is an extension of the job protec argument of the previous sec. From a theoretical point of view& of course& if foreign countries can produce a good at lower cost than we can& it is in our collective interest to obtain it from them. But workers counter by saying that the low wages of foreign workers means that foreign workers are exploited. To compete with foreign workers& American workers would have to accept comparably low wages. Ecomists generally reject this argument& ting that differences in wage rates generally reflect differences in worker productivity. 593
Consider the following example: Suppose U.S. workers in the tool industry earn $20 per hour while Indonesian workers in the tool industry earn only $2 per hour. If we assume that the tool industry is competitive& then wages in both countries are based on the marginal revenue product of the workers. The higher wage of U.S. workers must mean that they have a higher marginal product—they are more productive. The higher wages of U.S. workers need t mean that labor costs are higher in the United States than in Indonesia.
Further& we have seen that what matters for trade is comparative advantage& t comparative labor costs. If each na specializes in goods and services in which it has a comparative advantage—measured in the amount of other goods and services given up to produce them—then world produc& and therefore world consump& rises. By defini& each na will have a comparative advantage in something.
A particularly controversial issue in industrialized ecomies is outsourcing& in which firms in a developed country transfer some of their activities abroad in order to take advantage of lower labor costs in other countries. Generally speaking& the practice of outsourcing tends to reduce costs for the firms that do it. These firms then expand produc and increase domestic employment& as is discussed in the accompanying Case in Point essay.
Differences in Environmental Standards
Ather justifica for protecist measures is that free trade is unfair if it pits domestic firms against foreign rivals who do t have to adhere to the same regulatory standards. In the debate over NAFTA& for example& critics warned that Mexican firms& facing relatively lax pollu control standards& would have an unfair advantage over U.S. firms if restraints on trade between the two countries were removed.
Ecomic theory suggests& however& that differences in pollu-control policies can be an important source of comparative advantage. In general& the demand for environmental quality is positively related to income. People in higher-income countries demand higher environmental quality than do people in lower-income countries. This means that pollu has a lower cost in poorer than in richer countries. If an industry generates a great deal of pollu& it may be more efficient to locate it in a poor country than in a rich country. In effect& a poor country’s lower demand for environmental quality gives it a comparative advantage in produc of goods that generate a great deal of pollu.
Provided the benefits of pollu exceed the costs in the poor country& with the costs computed based on the preferences and incomes of people in that country& it makes sense for more of the good to be produced in the poor country and less in the rich country. Such an alloca leaves people in both countries better off than they would be otherwise. Then& as freer trade leads to higher incomes in the poorer countries& people there will also demand improvements in environmental quality.
Do ecomists support any restric on free internaal trade? Nearly all ecomists would say . The gains from trade are so large& and the cost of restraining it so high& that it is hard to find any satisfactory reason to restrict trade.
594 Key Takeaways
Protecist measures seek to limit the quantities of goods and services imported from foreign countries. They shift the supply curve for each of the goods or services protected to the left.
The primary means of protec are tariffs and quotas.
Antidumping proceedings have emerged as a common means of protec.
Voluntary export restrics are ather means of protec; they are rarely voluntary.
Other protecist measures can include safety standards& restrics on environmental quality& labeling requirements& and quality standards.
Protecist measures are sometimes justified using the infant industry argument& strategic trade policy& naal security protec& “cheap” foreign labor and outsourcing& and differences in environmental standards.

Case in Point: Outsourcing and Employment 595
figureure 17.12 Factory workers – CC BY-NC 2.0.
The phemen of outsourcing has become common as the Internet and other invas in communica have made it easier for firms to transfer aspects of their produc overseas. At the same time& countries such as India and China have invested heavily in educa and have produced a sizable workforce of professional people capable of filling relatively high level posis for firms in more developed countries.
The very idea of outsourcing rankles politicians on the left and on the right. In the United States& there have been numerous congressional hearings on outsourcing and proposals to block firms that engage in the practice from getting government contracts.
By outsourcing& firms are able to reduce their produc costs. As we have seen& a reduc in produc costs translates into increased output and falling prices. From a consumer’s point of view& then& outsourcing should be a very good thing. The worry many commentators express& however& is that outsourcing will decimate employment in the United States& particularly among high-level professionals. Matthew J. Slaughter& an ecomist at Dartmouth University& examined employment trends from 1991 to 2001 among multinaal U.S. firms that had outsourced jobs. Those firms outsourced 2.8 million jobs during the period.
Were the 2.8 million jobs simply lost? Mr. Slaughter points out that there are three reasons to expect that the firms that reduced produc costs by outsourcing would actually increase their domestic employment. First& by lowering cost& firms are likely to expand the quantity they produce. The foreign workers who were hired& who Mr. Slaughter refers to as “affiliate workers&” appeared to be complements to American workers rather than substitutes. If they are complements rather than substitutes& then outsourcing could lead to increased employment in the country that does the outsourcing.
A secd reason outsourcing could increase employment is that by lowering produc cost& firms that increase the scale of their operas through outsourcing need more domestic workers to sell the increased output& to coordinate its distribu& and to develop the infrastructure to handle all those goods.
Finally& firms that engage in outsourcing are also likely to increase the scope of their operas. They will need to hire addial people to explore other product development& to engage in research& and to seek out new markets for the firm’s output.
Thus& Mr. Slaughter argues that outsourcing may lead to increased employment because domestic workers are complements to foreign workers& because outsourcing expands the scale of a firm’s operas& and because it expands the scope of operas. What did the evidence show? Remember the 2.8 million jobs that multinaal firms based in the United States outsourced between 1991 and 2001? Employment at those same U.S. firms increased by 5.5 millionjobs during the period. Thus& with the phemena of complementarity& increases in scale& and increases of scope& each job outsourced led to almost two addial jobs in the United States. 596
The experience of two quite dissimilar firms illustrates the phemen. Wal-Mart began expanding its operas internaally in about 1990. Today& it manages its global operas from its headquarters in Bentonville& Arkansas& where it employs 15&000 people. Roughly 1&500 of these people coordinate the flow of goods among Wal-Mart’s stores throughout the world. Those 1&500 jobs would t exist were it t for globaliza. Xilinx& the high techlogy research and development firm& generates sales of about $1.5 billion per year. Sixty-five percent of its sales are generated outside the United States. But 80% of its employees are in the United States.
Outsourcing& then& generates jobs. It does t destroy them. Mr. Slaughter concludes: “Instead of lamenting ongoing foreign expansion of U.S. multinaals& if history is our guide then we should be encouraging it.”
Source: Matthew J. Slaughter& “Globaliza and Employment by U.S. Multinaals: A Framework and Facts&” Daily Tax Report (March 26& 2004): 1–12.

598 17.4 Review and Practice
Summary
In this chapter we have seen how internaal trade makes it possible for countries to improve on their domestic produc possibilities.
A country that is operating on its produc possibilities curve can obtain more of all goods by opening its markets to internaal trade. Free trade allows nas to consume goods beyond their domestic produc possibilities curve. If nas specialize in the produc of goods and services in which they have a comparative advantage& total output increases. Free trade enhances produc possibilities on a worldwide scale. It does t benefit everyone& however. Some workers and owners of other factors of produc will be hurt by free trade& at least in the short run.
Contrary to the implica of the model of specializa based on comparative advantage& t all trade is one-way trade. Two-way trade in the same goods may arise from varias in transporta costs and seasonal influences. Two-way trade in similar goods is often the result of imperfect competi. Much trade among high-income countries is two-way trade.
The imposi of trade barriers such as tariffs& antidumping proceedings& quotas& or voluntary export restrics raises the equilibrium price and reduces the equilibrium quantity of the restricted good. Although there are many arguments in favor of such restrics on free trade& ecomists generally are against protecist measures and supportive of free trade.

601 The Ecomics of the Environment
Start Up: A Market for Carbon Emissions
Emissions of carbon dioxide& a “greenhouse gas&” are limited by terms of the Kyoto accords& a treaty signed and ratified by most of the world’s nas. The treaty requires industrialized nas ratifying it to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide& which are thought to cause global warming& by 5.2% below their 1990 levels. The treaty also requires industrialized nas to assist developing nas with their efforts to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases. The vast majority of the world’s nas have ratified the accords; the United States is among a mirity of nas that are t participating in them.
The Kyoto accords require that each industrialized na specify quotas for each firm or organiza that emits greenhouse gases. Those that emit less than their quotas can sell their unused rights to emit gases to other firms or organizas. Any agent that wishes to exceed its quota must purchase rights from someone else. That exchange permits organizas that can meet their quotas at relatively low cost to sell rights to others for which reduc would be costly. The exchanges still allow the overall target to be met& but at much lower cost.
President George W. Bush’s predecessor& President Bill Clinton& signed the Kyoto agreement& but it was t ratified by the United States Senate. President Bush withdrew the United States from the agreement citing damage to the ecomy that implementa would cause& the fact that rapidly industrializing ecomies& such as China and India& are excluded& and inconclusive science. Despite this& many firms and other organizas in the United States have already agreed to limit their emissions of greenhouse gases. For the more than 100 members of the Chicago Climate Exchange (CCX)& companies and organizas including IBM& the Ford Motor Company& Motorola& and the cities of Chicago and Oakland& the idea of exchanging rights to dump greenhouse gases into the atmosphere is already a reality.
Members of the CCX& formed in 2003 by Richard Sandor& a commodities entrepreneur and ecomist who helped establish markets in financial futures& have pledged to reduce their emissions of greenhouse gases to an agreed target. If a member wishes to undertake a project that would generate addial carbon emissions& it purchases rights to the addial carbon from ather member. In its first nine months of opera& CCX members traded rights to more than 1&000&000 tons of carbon. The CCX quotas are far less stringent than are those of the Kyoto accords. The chief importance of CCX is that it establishes a model for the exchange of emissions rights should the United States sign the treaty.
The development of a market for pollu rights puts market forces to work in an effort to reduce the pressing problem of global warming. The European Union introduced exchanges in rights to emit greenhouse gases and issued quotas to firms for carbon dioxide emissions in its 25 member nas in 2005. Anticipating the program& firms began trading rights to emit carbon dioxide in 2004& when the European Climate Exchange was anunced. The price of the right to dump a metric ton of greenhouse gases was about $20. By 2008& the price had risen to $35 and rights to emit 295 million tons were traded on the ECX in June of that year. ECX Market Update& June 2008& http://www.ecx.eu. Fialka& “Russian Interest in Signing Kyoto Spurs Trading&” Wall Street Journal Online& June 1& 2004. The CCX has since formed a partnership with London’s Internaal Petroleum Exchange and the European Climate Exchange& so that European firms can exchange carbon rights on an internaal basis. 602
In this chapter we shall put the analytical tools we have developed to work on the problems of the environment. We will begin with an examina of problems of air and water pollu. We will look also at alternative regulatory approaches to environmental problems. Direct controls& in which government agencies tell people what they must do to reduce pollu& remain the primary means of government regula. Persuasion& or voluntary compliance with pollu reduc efforts& is also used. Two alternatives that ecomists advocate are taxes on pollutants and marketable pollu rights; such systems are gaining in importance.
Related issues include those of common property resources& those scarce resources for which property rights are defined& and exhaustible natural resources& those resources whose stocks decline as they are used. 603 18.1 Maximizing the Net Benefits of Pollu
Learning Objectives
Explain why pollu can be said to have benefits as well as costs and describe the nature of these benefits and costs.
Using marginal benefit and marginal cost curves& apply the marginal decision rule to show and explain what is meant by the efficient level of emissions and abatement.
Explain the Coase theorem and what it implies about the condis under which the private market is likely to achieve an efficient outcome.
We all pollute the environment. We do so t because we get some perverse satisfac from polluting but because activities that give us utility inevitably pollute. We do t drive our cars in order to dump carbon moxide into the air but because we gain utility from the transporta and convenience cars provide. Firms pollute the environment if doing so allows them to produce goods and services at lower cost.
The benefits we derive from pollu are indirect. We obtain them from other activities that generate pollu. But that is t unusual—there are many things we do because of the other benefits they produce. Firms benefit from hiring labor t because their owners enjoy hiring workers but because those workers produce output and profits. We purchase electricity t because we enjoy the feeling of having the stuff racing through wires in our house but because the electricity produces light& heat& and other services more cheaply than would alternatives such as candles or fires. In purchasing this electricity& of course& we are demanding a good whose produc inevitably degrades the environment. We pollute in the process of obtaining more of other goods and services we enjoy. We thus benefit from our pollu.
Of course& we suffer from the pollu we all generate as well. Smog-choked air damages our health and robs us of scenic views. We may t be able to fish or swim in polluted rivers. Just as the genera of pollu makes many of the activities we pursue less expensive& the fact that we have pollu increases many costs. Polluted rivers increase the cost of producing drinking water. Polluted air requires us to spend more on health care and to paint our buildings more often. Polluted soils produce less food.
Like any other activity& then& pollu has benefits as well as costs. The difficulty with pollu problems is that decision makers experience the benefits of their own choices to pollute the environment& but the costs spread to everyone who breathes the air or consumes the water. These costs are examples of external costs. Recall that external costs produce one type of market failure and that market failures lead to inefficiency in the alloca of resources. The environment presents us with an alloca problem in which decision makers are t faced with all the benefits and costs of their choices. Environmental resources will t& in such cases& be allocated efficiently.
Ecomists who examine and analyze environmental problems try to determine what an efficient alloca of the environment would most likely be—one that maximizes the difference between the total benefits and total costs of our pollu. 604
The basic problem of moving the ecomy from its current& inefficient solu& in which there is likely to be more pollu than is efficient& to the efficient solu. We have learned that private markets often fail to achieve efficient solus to environmental problems because property rights are difficult to define and to exchange. We will see& however& that environmental ecomists have devised invative ways to introduce property rights into environmental policy and to harness market forces to improve rather than degrade environmental quality.
Pollu and Scarcity
Pollu exists whenever human activity generates a sufficient concentra of a substance in the environment to cause harm to people or to resources valued by people. Many potentially harmful substances are natural parts of the environment& but they are t generally regarded as pollutants. Pollu is the product of people& t nature.
Pollu implies scarcity. If an activity emits harmful by-products into the environment& then the emission of the by-products is an alternative to some other activity. A scarcity problem exists at the point where harm begins.
A fire burning in a fireplace at a cabin in the forest whose smoke goes unticed does t suggest a scarcity problem. But when there are other people who will be harmed by the smoke& then one person’s enjoyment of a fire becomes an alternative to ather person’s enjoyment of fresh air. Fresh air has become scarce& and pollu has become an ecomic problem.
Ecomists generally argue that pollu that harms plants or animals imposes a cost if the plants or animals are valued by people. When a farmer uses a pesticide that damages ather farmer’s crop& for example& a pollu problem occurs. If an oil spill in the ocean damages sea animals that people care about& there is a pollu problem. It is& after all& people who make the choices that lead to pollu. It is people who can choose to limit their pollu. Ecomists therefore examine pollu problems from the perspective of the preferences of people.
The Efficient Level of Pollu
The efficient level of pollu is the quantity at which its total benefits exceed its total costs by the greatest possible amount. This occurs where the marginal benefit of an addial unit of pollu equals its marginal cost.
figureure 18.1 “Determining the Efficient Level of Pollu” shows how we can determine an efficient quantity of pollu. Suppose two neighbors in a remote mountain area& Mary and Jane& burn fires in their cabins that generate air pollu that harms two other individuals& Sam and Richard& who live downwind. We shall assume that Mary and Jane are the only polluters and that Sam and Richard are the only people harmed by the pollu. We shall igre& for example& the effect of Mary and Jane’s emissions on the possible problem of global warming. 605

Mary and Jane each benefit from polluting the environment by emitting smoke from their fires. In Panel (a)& we see that Mary’s demand curve for emitting smoke is given by DM and that Jane’s demand curve is given by DJ. To determine the total demand curve& DT& we determine the amount that each person will emit at various prices. At a price of $13 per day& for example& Mary will emit 20 pounds per day. Jane will emit 14 pounds per day& for a total of 34 pounds per day on demand curve DT. tice that if the price were $0 per unit& Mary would emit 40 pounds per day& Jane would emit 20& and emissions would total 60 pounds per day on curve DT. The marginal cost curve for pollu is determined in Panel (b) by taking the marginal cost curves for each person affected by the pollu. In this case& the only people affected are Sam and Richard. Sam’s marginal cost curve is MCS& and Richard’s marginal cost curve is MCR. Because Sam and Richard are each affected by the same pollu& we add their marginal cost curves vertically. For example& if the total quantity of the emissions is 34 pounds per day& the marginal cost of the 34th pound to Richard is $4& it is $9 to Sam& for a total marginal cost of the 34th unit of $13. In Panel (c)& we put DT and MCT together to find the efficient solu. The two curves intersect at a level of emissions of 34 pounds per day& which occurs at a price of $13 per pound.
Suppose& as is often the case& that mechanism exists to charge Mary and Jane for their emissions; they can pollute all they want and never have to compensate society (that is& pay Sam and Richard) for the damage they do. Alternatively& suppose there is mechanism for Sam and Richard to pay Mary and Jane to get them to reduce their pollu. In either situa& the pollu generated by Mary and Jane imposes an external cost on Sam and Richard. Mary and Jane will pollute up to the point that the marginal benefit of addial pollu to them has reached zero—that is& up to the point where the marginal benefit matches their marginal cost. They igre the external costs they impose on “society”—Sam and Richard.
Mary’s and Jane’s demand curves for pollu are shown in Panel (a). These demand curves& DM and DJ& show the quantities of emissions each generates at each possible price& assuming such a fee were assessed. At a price of $13 per unit& for example& Mary will emit 20 units of pollutant per period and Jane will emit 14. Total emissions at a price of $13 would be 34 units per period. If the price of emissions were zero& total emissions would be 60 units per period. In the absence of a fee& we would expect these individuals to emit a total of 60 units of pollutant per period. 606
Because Mary and Jane choose to pollute at the point that their marginal benefit equals that price. We can therefore interpret their demand curves as their marginal benefit curves for emissions. Their combined demand curve DT gives the marginal benefit to society (that is& Mary and Jane) of pollu. Each person in our problem& Mary& Jane& Sam& and Richard& follows the marginal decision rule and thus attempts to maximize utility.
In Panel (b) we see how much Sam and Richard are harmed; the marginal cost curves& MCS and MCR& measure their respective valuas of the harm imposed on them by each addial unit of emissions. tice that for a limited range& some emissions generate harm. At very low levels& neither Sam r Richard is even aware of the emissions. Richard begins to experience harm as the quantity of emissions goes above 5 pounds per period; it is here that pollu begins to occur. As emissions increase& the addial harm each unit creates becomes larger and larger—the marginal cost curves are upward sloping. The first traces of pollu may be only a mir inconvenience& but as pollu goes up& the problems it creates become more serious—and its marginal cost rises.
Because the same emissions affect both Sam and Richard& we add their marginal cost curves vertically to get their combined marginal cost curve MCT. The 34th unit of emissions& for example& imposes an addial cost of $9 on Sam and $4 on Richard. It thus imposes a total marginal cost of $13.
The efficient quantity of emissions is found at the intersec of the demand (DT) and marginal cost (MCT) curves in Panel (c) of figureure 18.1 “Determining the Efficient Level of Pollu”& with 34 units of the pollutant emitted. The marginal benefit of the 34th unit of emissions& as measured by the demand curve DT& equals its marginal cost& MCT& at that level. The quantity at which the marginal benefit curve intersects the marginal cost curve maximizes the net benefit of an activity.
We have already seen that in the absence of a mechanism to charge Mary and Jane for their emissions& they face a price of zero and would emit 60 units of pollutant per period. But that level of pollu is inefficient. Indeed& as long as the marginal cost of an addial unit of pollu exceeds its marginal benefit& as measured by the demand curve& there is too much pollu; the net benefit of emissions would be greater with a lower level of activity.
Just as too much pollu is inefficient& so is too little. Suppose Mary and Jane are t allowed to pollute—emissions equal zero. We see in Panel (c) that the marginal benefit of dumping the first unit of pollu is quite high; the marginal cost it imposes on Sam and Richard is zero. Because the marginal benefit of addial pollu exceeds its marginal cost& the net benefit to society would be increased by increasing the level of pollu. That is true at any level of pollu below 34 units& the efficient solu.
The that too little pollu could be inefficient may strike you as strange. To see the logic of this& imagine that the pollutant involved is carbon moxide& a pollutant emitted whenever combus occurs& and a deadly one. It is& for example& emitted when you drive a car. w suppose that emissions of carbon moxide were allowed. Among other things& this would require a ban on all driving. Surely the benefits of some driving would exceed the cost of the pollu created. The problem in pollu policy from an ecomic perspective is to find the quantity of pollu at which total benefits exceed total costs by the greatest possible amount—the solu at which marginal benefit equals marginal cost.
607 Property Rights and the Coase Theorem
The problem of getting the efficient amount of pollu arises because one owns the right to the air. If someone did& then that owner could decide how to use it. If a wner did t like the way the owner was using it& he or she could try to pay the owner to change the way the air was being used.
In our earlier example& if Mary and Jane own the right to the air& but Sam and Richard do t like how much Mary and Jane are polluting it& Sam and Richard can offer to pay Mary and Jane to cut back on the amount they are polluting. Alternatively& if Sam and Richard own the air& then in order to pollute it& Mary and Jane would have to compensate the owners. Bargaining among the affected parties& if costless& would lead to the efficient amount of pollu. Costless bargaining requires that all parties kw the source of the pollu and are able to monitor the quantity emitted by each agent.
Specifically& suppose Mary and Jane own the right to dump pollutants into the air and had been emitting 60 units of the pollu per day. If Sam and Richard offer to pay them $13 for each unit of pollutant they cut back& Mary and Jane will reduce their pollu to 34 units& since the marginal benefit to them of the 35th to 60th unit is less than $13. Sam and Richard are better off since the marginal cost of those last 26 units of pollu is greater than $13 per unit. The efficient outcome of 34 units of pollu is thus achieved. Mary and Jane could reduce their emissions by burning their fires for less time& by selecting more efficient fireplaces& or by other means. Many people& for example& have reduced their emissions by changing to gas-burning fireplaces rather than burning wood.
While the well-being of the affected parties is t independent of who owns the property right (each would be better off owning rather than t owning the right)& the establishment of who owns the air leads to a solu that solves the externality problem and leads to an efficient market outcome. The proposi that if property rights are well defined and if bargaining is costless& the private market can achieve an efficient outcome regardless of which of the affected parties holds the property rights is kwn as the Coase theorem& named for the bel prize-winning ecomist Ronald Coase who generally is credited with this idea.
Suppose instead that Sam and Richard own the right to the air. They could charge Mary and Jane $13 per unit of pollu emitted. Mary and Jane would willingly pay for the right to emit 34 units of pollu& but t for any more& since beyond that amount the marginal benefit of each unit of pollu emitted is less than $13. Sam and Richard would willingly accept payments for 34 units of pollu at $13 each since the marginal cost to them of each of those units is less than $13.
In most cases& however& Coase stressed that the condis for private parties to achieve an efficient outcome on their own are t present. Property rights may t be defined. Even if one party owns a right& enforcement may be difficult. Suppose Sam and Richard own the right to clean air but many people& t just two as in our example& contribute to polluting it. Would each producer that pollutes have to strike a deal with Sam and Richard? Could the government enforce all those deals? And what if there are many owners as well? Enforcement becomes increasingly difficult and striking deals becomes more and more costly. Finally& monitoring is extremely difficult in most environmental problems. While it is generally possible to detect the presence of pollutants& determining their source is virtually impossible. And determining who is harmed and by how much is a monumental undertaking in most pollu problems.
Nevertheless& Coase’s analysis has been ermously influential in leading ecomists toward thinking about approaches to environmental problems that attempt to use the establishment of property rights and market mechanisms in various ways to bring about the efficient market outcome. Before considering alternative ways of controlling pollu& we look first at how the benefits and costs might be measured so that we have a better sense of what the efficient solu is. 608
Ather insight that comes from Coase’s analysis is that the of “harm” is a reciprocal one. In our example& it is tempting to conclude that Mary and Jane& by burning fires in their fireplaces& are “harming” Sam and Richard. But if Sam and Richard were t located downwind of the smoke& there would be harm. In fact& Mr. Coase insists that the harm cant be attributed to one party or ather. Sam and Richard “cause” the harm by locating downwind of the fireplaces. While there is clearly harm in this situa& we could as easily attribute it to either the generators of the smoke or the recipients of the smoke. Before Coase wrote his article& “The Problem of Social Cost” in 1960& the general presump was that decision makers such as Mary and Jane “caused” the harm and that they should be taxed for the costs they impose. Mr. Coase pointed out the alternative that Sam and Richard could avoid the harm by moving. Indeed& all sorts of alternative solus come to mind even in this simple example. Mary and Jane could select types of wood that emit less smoke. They could use fireplaces that emit less smoke. They could make arrangements to time their burning to minimize the total amount of smoke that affects Sam and Richard. The goal& Coase said& is to select the most efficient from the alternatives available (Coase& R. H.& 1960).
Consider a different problem. Suppose that an airport has been built several miles outside the developed area of a small city. one lives close eugh to the airport to be “harmed” by the ise inevitably generated by the opera of the airport. As time passes& people are likely to build houses near the airport to take advantage of jobs at the airport or to gain easy access to it. Those people will w be “harmed” by ise from the airport. But what is the cause of this harm? By defini& there was “harm” before people started living close to the airport. True& it is the airport that generates the ise. But the ise causes harm only because people w live near it. Just as Mary and Jane’s campfires only generate “harm” if someone is downwind of the smoke& the ise from the airport causes damage only if someone lives near the airport. The problem of the ise could be mitigated in several ways. First& people could have chosen t to live near the airport. Once they have chosen to live near the airport& they could reduce the ise with better insula or with better windows. Alternatively& the airport management could choose different flight patterns to reduce ise that affects neighboring homeowners. It is always the case that there are several potential ways of mitigating the effects of airport operas; the ecomic problem is to select the most efficient from among those alternatives.
The Measurement of Benefits and Costs
Saying that the efficient level of pollu occurs at a certain rate of emissions& as we have done so far& is one thing. Determining the actual posis of the demand and marginal cost curves that define that efficient solu is quite ather. Ecomists have devised a variety of methods for measuring these curves.
609 Benefits: The Demand for Emissions
A demand curve for emitting pollutants shows the quantity of emissions demanded per unit of time at each price. It can& as we have seen& be taken as a marginal benefit curve for emitting pollutants.
The general approach to estimating demand curves involves observing quantities demanded at various prices together with the values of other determinants of demand. In most pollu problems& however& the price charged for emitting pollutants has always been zero—we simply do t kw how the quantity of emissions demanded will vary with price.
One approach to estimating the demand curve for pollu utilizes the fact that this demand occurs because pollu makes other activities cheaper. If we kw how much the emission of one more unit of a pollutant saves& then we can infer how much consumers or firms would pay to dump it.
Suppose& for example& that there is program to control automobile emissions—motorists face a price of zero for each unit of pollu their cars emit. Suppose that a particular motorist’s car emits an average of 10 pounds of carbon moxide per week. Its owner could reduce emissions to 9 pounds per week at a cost of $1 per week. This $1 is the marginal cost of reducing emissions from 10 to 9 pounds per week. It is also the maximum price the motorist would pay to increase emissions from 9 to 10 pounds per week—it is the marginal benefit of that last pound of pollu. We say that it is the maximum price because if asked to pay more& the motorist would choose to reduce emissions at a cost of $1 instead.
w suppose that emissions have been reduced to 9 pounds per week and that the motorist could reduce them further at an addial cost of $2 per week. The marginal cost of reducing emissions from 9 to 8 pounds per week is $2. Alternatively& this is the maximum price the motorist would be willing to pay to increase emissions to 9 from 8 pounds; it is the marginal benefit of the 9th pound of pollu. Again& if asked to pay more than $2& the motorist would choose to reduce emissions to 8 pounds per week instead. 610
figureure 18.2 Abatement Costs and Demand
A car emits an average of 10 pounds of CO per week when restrics are imposed—when the price of emissions is zero. The marginal cost of abatement (MCA) is the cost of eliminating a unit of emissions; this is the interpreta of the curve when read from right to left. The same curve can be read from left to right as the marginal benefit of emissions (MBE).
We can thus think of the marginal benefit of an addial unit of pollu as the added cost of t emitting it. It is the saving a polluter enjoys by dumping addial pollu rather than paying the cost of preventing its emission. figureure 18.2 “Abatement Costs and Demand” shows this dual interpreta of cost and benefit. Initially& our motorist emits 10 pounds of carbon moxide per week. Reading from right to left& the curve measures the marginal costs of pollu abatement (MCA). We see that the marginal cost of abatement rises as emissions are reduced. That makes sense; the first reducs in emissions will be achieved through relatively simple means such as modifying one’s driving technique to minimize emissions (such as accelerating more slowly)& or getting tune-ups more often. Further reducs& however& might require burning more expensive fuels or installing expensive pollu-control equipment.
Read from left to right& the curve in figureure 18.2 “Abatement Costs and Demand” shows the marginal benefit of addial emissions (MBE). Its negative slope suggests that the first units of pollu emitted have very 601high marginal benefit; however& its marginal benefit falls—the cost of preventing these units of pollu becomes quite low. 611
Ecomists have also measured demand curves for emissions by using surveys in which polluters are asked to report the costs to them of reducing their emissions. In cases in which polluters are charged for the emissions they create& the marginal benefit curve can be observed directly.
As we saw in figureure 18.1 “Determining the Efficient Level of Pollu”& the marginal benefit curves of individual polluters are added horizontally to obtain a market demand curve for pollu. This curve measures the addial benefit to society of each addial unit of pollu.
The Marginal Cost of Emissions
Pollutants harm people and the resources they value. The marginal cost curve for a pollutant shows the addial cost imposed by each unit of the pollutant. As we saw in figureure 18.1 “Determining the Efficient Level of Pollu”& the marginal cost curves for all the individuals harmed by a particular pollutant are added vertically to obtain the marginal cost curve for the pollutant.
Like the marginal benefit curve for emissions& the marginal cost curve can be interpreted in two ways& as suggested in figureure 18.3 “The Marginal Cost of Emissions and the Marginal Benefit of Abatement”. When read from left to right& the curve measures the marginal cost of addial units of emissions (MCE). If increasing the monthly emissions from four pounds of carbon moxide per week to five pounds of carbon moxide per week imposes an external cost of $2& though& the marginal benefit of t being exposed to that unit of pollutant must be $2. The marginal cost curve can thus be read from right to left as a marginal benefit curve for abating emissions (MBA). This marginal benefit curve is& in effect& the demand curve for cleaner air. 612
figureure 18.3 The Marginal Cost of Emissions and the Marginal Benefit of Abatement
The marginal cost of the first few units of emissions is zero and then rises once emissions begin to harm people. That is the point at which the air becomes a scarce resource. Read from left to right the curve gives the marginal cost of emissions (MCE). Read from right to left& the curve gives the marginal benefit of abatement (MBA).
Ecomists estimate the marginal cost curve of pollu in several ways. One is to infer it from the demand for goods for which environmental quality is a complement. Ather is to survey people& asking them what pollu costs—or what they would pay to reduce it. Still ather is to determine the costs of damages created by pollu directly.
For example& environmental quality is a complement of housing. The demand for houses in areas with cleaner air is greater than the demand for houses in areas that are more polluted. By observing the relaship between house prices and air quality& ecomists can learn the value people place on cleaner air—and thus the cost of dirtier air. Studies have been conducted in cities all over the world to determine the relaship between air quality and house prices so that a measure of the demand for cleaner air can be made. They show that increased pollu levels result in lower house values (Becker& N. and Doron Laee& 2003).
Surveys are also used to assess the marginal cost of emissions. The fact that the marginal cost of an addial unit of pollu can be determined in several ways. Respondents can be asked how much they would be harmed by an increase in emissions& or they can be asked what they would pay for a reduc in emissions. Ecomists often use both kinds of quess in surveys designed to determine marginal costs. 613
A third kind of cost estimate is based on objects damaged by pollu. Increases in pollu& for example& cause buildings to be painted more often; the increased cost of painting is one measure of the cost of added pollu.
While all of the attempts to measure cost are imperfect& the alternative is to t try to quantify cost at all. To ecomists& such an ostrich-like approach of sticking one’s head in the sand would be unacceptable.
The Efficient Level of Emissions and Abatement
Whether ecomists measure the marginal benefits and marginal costs of emissions or& alternatively& the marginal benefits and marginal costs of abatement& the policy implicas are the same from an ecomic perspective. As shown in Panel (a) of figureure 18.4 “The Efficient Level of Emissions and Pollu Abatement”& applying the marginal decision rule in the case of emissions suggests that the efficient level of pollu occurs at six pounds of CO emitted per week. At any lower level& the marginal benefits of the pollu would outweigh the marginal costs. At a higher level& the marginal costs of the pollu would outweigh the marginal benefits. 614
figureure 18.4 The Efficient Level of Emissions and Pollu Abatement
Panel (a) shows the marginal benefit of emissions (MBE) and the marginal cost of emissions (MCE). The efficient solu occurs at the intersec of the two curves. Here& the efficient quantity of emissions is six pounds of CO per week. In Panel (b)& we have the same curves read from right to left. The marginal cost curve for emissions becomes the marginal benefit of abatement (MBA). The marginal benefit curve for emissions becomes the marginal cost of abatement (MCA). With abatement program& emissions total ten pounds of CO per week. The efficient degree of abatement is to reduce emissions by four pounds of CO per week to six pounds per week.
615
As shown in Panel (b) of figureure 18.4 “The Efficient Level of Emissions and Pollu Abatement”& applica of the marginal decision rule suggests that the efficient level of abatement effort is to reduce pollu by 4 pounds of CO produced per week. That is& reduce the level of pollu from the 10 pounds per week that would occur at zero price to 6 pounds per week. For any greater effort at abating the pollu& the marginal cost of the abatement efforts would exceed the marginal benefit.
Key Takeaways
Pollu is related to the concept of scarcity. The existence of pollu implies that an environmental resource has alternative uses and is thus scarce.
Pollu has benefits as well as costs; the emission of pollutants benefits people by allowing other activities to be pursued at lower costs. The efficient rate of emissions occurs where the marginal benefit of emissions equals the marginal cost they impose.
The marginal benefit curve for emitting pollutants can also be read from right to left as the marginal cost of abating emissions. The marginal cost curve for increased emission levels can also be read from right to left as the demand curve for improved environmental quality.
The Coase theorem suggests that if property rights are well-defined and if transacs are costless& then the private market will reach an efficient solu. These condis& however& are t likely to be present in typical environmental situas. Even if such condis do t exist& Coase’s arguments still yield useful insights to the mitiga of environmental problems.
Surveys are sometimes used to measure the marginal benefit curves for emissions and the marginal cost curves for increased pollu levels. Marginal cost curves may also be inferred from other relaships. Two that are commonly used are the demand for housing and the relaship between pollu and produc.

Case in Point: Estimating a Demand Curve for Environmental Quality
figureure 18.5 Amsterdam New York – Toxic Ghost Town Amsterdam New York – public domain.
617
How do ecomists estimate demand curves for environmental quality? One recent example comes from work by Louisiana State University ecomist David M. Brasington and Auburn University ecomist Diane Hite. Using data from Ohio’s six major metropolitan areas (Akron& Cincinnati& Cleveland& Columbus& Dayton& and Toledo)& the ecomists studied the relaship between house prices and the distance between individual houses and hazardous waste sites. From this& they were able to estimate the demand curve for environmental quality—at least in terms of the demand for locas farther from environmental hazards.
The ecomists used actual real estate transacs in 1991 to get data on house prices. In that year& there were 119 hazardous sites in the six metropolitan areas. The study was based on 44&255 houses. The median distance between a house and a hazardous site was 1.08 miles. The two ecomists found& as one would expect& that house prices were higher the greater the distance between the house and a hazardous site. All other variables unchanged& increasing the distance from a house to a hazardous site by 10% increased house value by 0.3%.
Other characteristics of the demand curve shed light on the relaship between environmental quality and other goods. For example& the study showed that people substitute house size for environmental quality. A house closer to a hazardous waste site is cheaper; people take advantage of the lower price of such sites to purchase larger houses.
While house size and environmental quality were substitutes& school quality& measured by student scores on achievement tests& was a complement. If the price of school quality were to fall by 10%& household would buy 8% more environmental quality. The cross-price elasticity between environmental quality and school quality was thus estimated to be −0.80.
There is marketplace for environmental quality. Estimating the demand curve for such quality requires ecomists to examine other data to try to infer what the demand curve is. The study by Professors Brasington and Hite illustrates the use of an examina of an actual market& the market for houses& to determine characteristics of the demand curve for environmental quality.
Source: David M. Brasington and Diane Hite& “Demand for Environmental Quality: A Spatial Hedonic Analysis&” Regional Science & Urban Ecomics& 35(1) (January 2005): 57–82.

619 18.2 Alternatives in Pollu Control
Learning Objectives
Explain why command-and-control approaches to reducing pollu are inefficient.
Explain what is meant by incentive approaches to pollu reduc and discuss examples of them& explaining their advantages and disadvantages.
Suppose that the goal of public policy is to reduce the level of emissions. Three types of policy alternatives can be applied. The first is persuasion—people can be exhorted to reduce their emissions. The secd relies on direct controls& and the third uses incentives to induce reducs in emissions.
Moral Suasion
Back in the days when preventing forest fires was a goal of public policy& a cartoon character called Smokey Bear once asked us to be careful with fire. Signs everywhere remind us t to litter. Some communities have mounted campaigns that admonish us to “Give a hoot—don’t pollute.”
These efforts to influence our choices are examples of moral suasion& an effort to change people’s behavior by appealing to their sense of moral values. Moral suasion is widely used as a tactic in attempting to reduce pollu. It has& for example& been fairly successful in campaigns against littering& which can be considered a form of pollu. Efforts at moral suasion are t generally successful in reducing activities that pollute the air and water. Pleas that people refrain from driving on certain days when pollu is very great& for example& achieve very little compliance.
Moral suasion appears to be most effective in altering behaviors that are t already widespread and for which the cost of compliance is low. It is easy to be careful with one’s fires or to avoid littering.
Moral suasion does t& however& appear to lead to significant changes in behavior when compliance costs are high or when the activity is already widely practiced. It is therefore t likely to be an effective tool for reducing most forms of pollu.
Command and Control
In the most widely used regulatory approach to environmental pollu& a government agency tells a polluting agent how much pollu it can emit or requires the agent to use a particular produc method aimed at reducing emissions. This approach& in which government directs the decisions of those whose emissions must be adjusted& is called the command-and-control approach. 620
Ecomists are generally critical of the command-and-control approach for two reasons. First& it achieves a given level of emissions reduc at a higher cost than what would be required to achieve that amount of reduc if market incentives (discussed below) were implemented. secd& it gives polluters incentive to explore techlogical and other changes that might reduce the demand for emissions.
Suppose two firms& A and B& each dump 500 tons of a certain pollutant per month and that there is fee imposed (that is& the price for their emissions equals zero). Total emissions for the two firms thus equal 1&000 tons per month. The pollu control authority decides to cut this in half and orders each firm to reduce its emissions to 250 tons per month& for a total reduc of 500 tons. This is a command-and-control regula because it specifies the amount of reduc each firm must make. Although it may seem fair to require equal reducs from the two firms& this approach is likely to generate excessive costs.
Suppose that Firm A is quite old and that the reduc in emissions to 250 tons per period would be extremely costly. Suppose that removing the 251st ton costs this firm $1&000 per month. Put ather way& the marginal benefit to Firm A of emitting the 251st ton would be $1&000.
Suppose Firm B& a much newer firm& already has some pollu-control equipment in place. Reducing emissions to 250 tons imposes a cost& but a much lower cost than to Firm A. Indeed& suppose Firm B could reduce its emissions to 249 tons at an addial cost of $100; the marginal benefit to Firm B of emitting the 249th ton is $100.
If two firms have different marginal benefits of emissions& the alloca of resources is inefficient. The same level of emissions could be achieved at a lower cost. Suppose& for example& Firm A is permitted to increase its emissions to 251 tons while Firm B reduces emissions to 249. Firm A saves $1&000& while the cost to Firm B is just $100. Society achieves a net gain of $900& and the level of emissions remains at 500 tons per month.
As long as Firm A’s marginal benefit of emissions exceeds Firm B’s& a saving is realized by shifting emissions from B to A. At the point at which their marginal benefits are equal& further reduc in the cost of achieving a given level of emissions is possible& and the alloca of emissions is efficient. When a given reduc in emissions is achieved so that the marginal benefit of an addial unit of emissions is the same for all polluters& it is a least-cost reduc in emissions. A command-and-control approach is unlikely to achieve a least-cost reduc in emissions.
The inefficiency of command-and-control regula is important for two reasons. First& of course& it wastes scarce resources. If the same level of air or water quality could be achieved at a far lower cost& then surely it makes sense to use the cheaper method. Perhaps even more significant& reliance on command-and-control regula makes environmental quality far more expensive than it needs to be—and that is likely to result in an unwillingness to achieve the improvements that would be ecomically efficient.
There is a further difficulty with the command-and-control approach. Once firms A and B have been told to reduce their emissions to 250 tons per period& neither firm has an incentive to try to do better. Neither firm will engage in research seeking to reduce its emissions below 250 tons. 621
The difficulties of the command-and-control approach become even clearer when one imagines what it would be like if a similar method were in use for other resource alloca problems. Suppose& for example& that labor were allocated according to a command-and-control mechanism. Rather than leaving labor alloca to the marketplace& suppose that firms were simply told how much labor to use. Such a system would clearly be unworkable.
Incentive Approaches
Markets allocate resources efficiently when the price system confronts decision makers with the costs and benefits of their decisions. Prices create incentives—they give producers an incentive to produce more and consumers an incentive to ecomize. Regulatory efforts that seek to create market-like incentives to encourage reducs in pollu& but that allow individual decision makers to determine how much to pollute& are called incentive approaches.
Emissions Taxes
One incentive approach to pollu control relies on taxes. If a tax is imposed on each unit of emissions& polluters will reduce their emissions until the marginal benefit of emissions equals the tax& and a least-cost reduc in emissions is achieved.
Emissions taxes are widely used in Europe. France& for example& has enacted taxes on the sulfur dioxide and nitrous oxide emissions of power plants and other industrial firms. Spain has imposed taxes on the dumping of pollutants into the country’s waterways. Emissions taxes have long been imposed on firms that dump pollutants into some river systems in Europe.
Emissions taxes are also being used in ecomies making the transi from socialism to a market system. In China& taxes are used to limit the emission by firms of water pollutants. By law& 80% of the money collected through these taxes goes back to the firms themselves for emissions control projects. The tax in China is a rudimentary one. The level of a firm’s emissions is determined by visual inspec of the water just downstream from the point at which the firm emits pollutants. Taxes are imposed based on a guess as to how much the firm has emitted. A similar approach is used in China to limit emissions of particulate matter& an important air pollutant. While this method appears primitive& it is nevertheless successful. During the 1990s& China had the fastest growing ecomy in the world. Total ecomic activity increased in China at an annual rate of about 10% per year. Despite this phemenal increase in ecomic activity& internaal estimates of China’s emissions of particulates suggest that they were down 50% during the decade. China’s emissions of effluents were unchanged during this period of phemenal growth.
Taxes are also used to limit pollu in the countries of the former Soviet Union. Rather than basing taxes on an estimate of marginal cost& taxes are set according to complicated engineering formulae. In Lithuania& for example& the tax on sulfide emissions in the water has been set at several million dollars per ton. Needless to say& that tax is t even collected. 622
The important role for pollu taxes in improving environmental quality is often misunderstood. For example& the Argentine government in the 1990s attempted to introduce pollu taxes to limit the dumping of effluents in the country’s rivers. Environmental groups went to federal court& charging that the taxes constituted a “license to pollute.” The unfortunate result was that the Argentine government withdrew its effort to control pollu through taxa without finding an adequate substitute policy.1
An emissions tax requires& of course& that a polluter’s emissions be monitored. The polluter is then charged a fee equal to the tax per unit times the quantity of emissions. The tax clearly gives the polluter an incentive to reduce emissions. It also ensures that reducs will be accomplished by those polluters that can achieve them at the lowest cost. Polluters for whom reducs are most costly will generally find it cheaper to pay the emissions tax.
In cases where it is difficult to monitor emissions& a tax could be imposed indirectly. Consider& for example& farmers’ use of fertilizers and pesticides. Rain may wash some of these materials into local rivers& polluting the water. Clearly& it would be virtually impossible to monitor this ruff and assess responsible farmers a charge for their emissions. But it would be possible to levy a tax on these materials when they are sold& confronting farmers with a rough measure of the cost of the pollu their use of these materials imposes.
Marketable Pollu Permits
An alternative to emissions taxes is marketable pollu permits& which allow their owners to emit a certain quantity of pollu during a particular period. The introduc to this chapter dealt with an example of marketable pollu permits; each of the permits to dump a metric ton of greenhouse gases that is purchased results in a reduc in the cost of meeting the goal of reducing the emissions of these gases.
To see how this works& suppose that Firms A and B are again told that they must reduce their emissions to 250 tons of a pollutant per month. This time& however& they are given 250 permits each—one permit allows the emission of one ton per month. They can trade their permits; a firm that emits less than its allotted 250 tons can sell some of its permits to ather firm that wants to emit more.
We saw that Firm B can reduce its emissions below 250 tons for a much lower cost than Firm A. For example& it could reduce its emissions to 249 tons for $100. Firm A would be willing to pay $1&000 for the right to emit the 251st ton of emissions. Clearly& a mutually profitable exchange is possible. In fact& as long as their marginal benefits of pollu differ& the firms can profit from exchange. Equilibrium will be achieved at the least-cost solu at which the marginal benefits for both firms are equal.
One virtue of using marketable permits is that this approach represents only a modest departure from tradial command-and-control regula. Once a polluter has been told to reduce its emissions to a certain quantity& it has a right to emit that quantity. Polluters will exchange rights only if doing so increases their utility or profits—allowing rights to be exchanged can only make them better off. Ather benefit& of course& is that exchanges allow a shift from the inefficient alloca created by command-and-control regula to an efficient alloca in which pollu is reduced at the lowest possible cost. Finally& each firm will have an incentive to explore ways to reduce its emissions further& either to be able to sell more rights or to require purchasing fewer permits.
623 Merits of Incentive Approaches
Incentive systems& either emissions taxes or tradable permits& can achieve reducs in emissions at a far lower cost than command-and-control regula. Even more important& however& are the long-run incentives they create for techlogical change. A firm that is ordered to reduce its emissions to a certain level has incentive to do better& whereas a firm facing an emissions tax has a constant incentive to seek out new ways to lower its emissions and thus lower its taxes. Similarly& a firm faces a cost for using an emissions permit—the price that could be obtained from selling the permit—so it will seek ways to reduce emissions. As firms discover new ways to reduce their costs of reducing emissions& the demand for emissions permits will fall& lowering the efficient quantity of emissions—and improving environmental quality even further.
Public Policy and Pollu: The Record
Federal efforts to control air and water pollu in the United States have produced mixed results. Air quality has generally improved; water quality has improved in some respects but deteriorated in others.
