Public policy has generally stressed command-and-control approaches to air and water pollu. To reduce air pollu& the EPA sets air quality standards that regions must achieve& then tells polluters what adjustments they must make in order to meet the standards. For water pollu& the Environmental Protec Agency (EPA) has set emissions limits based on the techlogies it considers reasonable to require of polluters. If the implementa of a particular techlogy will reduce a polluter’s emissions by 20%& for example& the EPA will require a 20% reduc in emissions. Naal standards have been imposed; effort has been made to consider the benefits and costs of pollu in individual streams. Further& the EPA’s techlogy-based approach pays little atten to actual water quality—and has produced few gains.
Moreover& environmental problems go beyond naal borders. For example& sulfur dioxide emitted from plants in the United States can result in acid rain in Canada and elsewhere. Ather possible pollu problem that extends across naal borders is suggested by the global warming hypothesis.
Many scientists have argued that increasing emissions of greenhouse gases& caused partly by the burning of fossil fuels& trap ever more of the sun’s energy and make the planet warmer. Global warming& they argue& could lead to flooding of coastal areas& losses in agricultural produc& and the elimina of many species. If this global warming hypothesis is correct& then the problem of greenhouse gas emissions requires a global solu. 625
At the 1997 United Nas conference in Kyoto& Japan& the industrialized countries agreed to cuts in carbon dioxide emissions of 5.2% below the 1990 level by 2010. At the 1998 conference in Bues Aires& Argentina& 170 countries agreed on a two-year ac plan for designing mechanisms to reduce emissions and procedures to encourage transfers of new energy techlogies to developing countries.
While the delegates to the conferences sign the various protocols& countries are t bound by them until ratified by appropriate governmental bodies. By 2005& the vast majority of the world’s nas had ratified the agreement. The United States had neither signed r ratified the agreement.
Debates at these conferences have been over the extent to which developing countries should be required to limit their emissions and over the role that market mechanisms should play. Developing countries argue that their share in total emissions is fairly small and that it is unfair to ask them to give up ecomic growth& given their lower income levels. As for how emissions reducs will be achieved& the United States has been the strongest advocate for emissions trading in which each country would receive a certain number of tradable emissions permits. This provision has been incorporated in the agreement.
That market approaches have entered the naal and internaal debates on dealing with environmental problems& and to a large extent have even been used& demonstrates the power of ecomic analysis. Ecomists have long argued that as pollu-control authorities replace command-and-control strategies with incentive approaches& society will reap huge savings. The ecomic argument has rested on ackwledging the opportunity cost of addressing environmental concerns and thus has advocated policies that achieve improvements in the environment in the least costly ways.
Key Takeaways
Public sector interven is generally needed to move the ecomy toward the efficient solu in pollu problems.
Command-and-control approaches are the most widely used methods of public sector interven& but they are inefficient.
The exchange of pollu rights can achieve a given reduc in emissions at the lowest cost possible. It also creates incentives to reduce pollu demand through techlogical change.
Tax policy can also achieve a least-cost reduc in emissions.

Case in Point: Road Pricing in Singapore 626
figureure 18.8 William towidagdo – Traffic in Singapore – CC BY 2.0.
The urban highways of virtually every city in the world are heavily congested in what is fancifully referred to as the “rush hour.” Traffic during this period hardly rushes. The problem of traffic conges is analogous to the problem of pollu& and it lends itself to the same solu.
Suppose that you are driving into any major city on a weekday at eight o’clock in the morning. The highway is congested when you drive onto it. Your car adds to that conges. You& of course& experience the average level of conges. But& your car slows every car behind you on the highway by a small amount. Multiplying that extra slowing by the number of cars behind you gives the marginal delay of adding your own car to an already congested highway. That marginal cost is many times greater than the average cost that you actually face. The result is an inefficient solu in which roads are congested far beyond the point that would be ecomically efficient. The late William Vickrey& who won the bel Prize for his work in the ecomics of public finance& advocated a system of road pricing that would put an end to congested highways.
Mr. Vickrey’s dream is a reality in Singapore. The island-na’s 700&000 cars are each required to subscribe to the Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) system and to have an ERP card on their windshield. Further& each driver is required to maintain a deposit of electronic cash in the card. Tolls are charged during rush hour for the highways leading into the downtown area. There is also a charge for using downtown streets. Tolls range from $0.50 to $1.00 and are only levied if the road threatens to become congested. Using highways and streets is free at other times. ERP managers adjust the tolls to avoid “jam-ups&” as they are called in Singapore. Managers attempt to keep traffic flowing at 30 to 40 mph on highways and 15 to 20 mph on downtown streets.
When a car passes an electronic gurney& it automatically takes the charge out of the ERP card on the windshield. When a charge is taken from the card& the driver hears a beep. If the card balance falls below $5& several beeps are heard. The cards can be placed in ATMs to put addial funds in them. A car that does t have eugh money in its card is photographed and the owner of the car receives a $45 cita in the mail. The tolls keep casual drivers off the roads during rush hour. Commuters generally find it cheaper to use the island’s excellent rapid transit system.
The system is t universally popular. People in Singapore refer to the system as “Eternally Raising Prices.” The manager of the system& Hiok Seng Tan& rejects the criticism. “It’s t just a system to get more money of Singaporeans&” he told the Boston Globe. In fact& the system takes in only $44 million per year; the money is used to maintain the system.
Singapore’s system is an example of a price system to manage what is& in effect& a pollu problem. It appears to be effective. Jam-ups are uncommon. Would such a system work in other areas? The idea is t politically popular. Gregory B. Christainsen& a professor of ecomics at California State University at East Bay& tes that Singapore is dominated by a single party and quess whether other urban areas are ready for the approach. Still& the system works and the concept is one more urban areas should consider. 627
Sources: Alex Beam& “Where Traffic Has Been Tamed&” Boston Globe& (May 2& 2004): M-7; Gregory B. Christainsen& “Road Pricing in Singapore after 30 Years&” Cato Journal& 26(1) (Winter 2006): 71–88.

628 18.3 Review and Practice
Summary
Pollu is a by-product of human activity. It occurs when the environment becomes scarce—when dumping garbage imposes a cost. There are benefits as well as costs to pollu; the efficient quantity of pollu occurs where the difference between total benefits and total costs is maximized. This solu is achieved where the marginal benefit of addial pollu equals the marginal cost. We have seen that an alternative approach shows that efficiency is also achieved where the marginal benefit of pollu abatement equals the marginal cost of abatement.
Ecomists measure the benefits of pollu in terms of the costs of t dumping the pollu. The same curve can be read from left to right as the marginal benefit curve for emissions and from right to left as the marginal cost curve for abatement.
The costs of pollu are measured in two ways. One is through direct surveys. Respondents can be asked how much compensa they would be willing to accept in exchange for a reduc in environmental pollu; alternatively& they can be asked how much they would pay for an improvement in environmental quality. A secd approach infers the marginal cost of increased pollu from other relaships. The effects of pollu on house prices or rental values& for example& allow ecomists to estimate the value people place on environmental quality. Pollu costs can also be estimated on the basis of the costs they impose on firms in produc.
Three types of policies are available to reduce pollu. Moral suasion is sometimes used& but it is effective only under limited condis. Command-and-control regula is used most commonly& but it is likely to be inefficient. It also fails to provide incentives for techlogical change in the long run. The most promising policies are the incentive approaches& which include emissions taxes and marketable pollu permits. Both can be designed to reduce emissions at the lowest cost possible& and both create an incentive for firms to search out new and cheaper ways to reduce emissions.
Although public policy has stressed command-and-control methods in the past& pollu rights exchanges are w being introduced. Past policies may have been inefficient& but they have succeeded in improving air quality& at least in the na’s cities.
